title: Measuring things: units, instruments, and why a coast has more than one length

summary.text: Old school books say India's coast is 7,516 kilometres long. A newer count says 11,098 kilometres. The coast did not grow, so how can both be right? In this lesson you find out what measuring is, meet the units for length, mass, volume, time and temperature, and learn to choose and read the right instrument. You build a water clock from a bottle, test whether it keeps steady time, and ask what a measurement can tell us and what it cannot.
summary.art: A map of India's coastline drawn twice, once with a few long straight steps and once with many short steps that follow every bend.

intro.hook: Measure the width of a table in hand spans. Now ask a grown-up to measure the same table in their hand spans. You get two different numbers for one table. Which number is the table's real width?
intro.text: Neither number is wrong. Each of you compared the table with your own hand and counted. The table stayed the same, and the hands were different. This small puzzle is the reason people invented the metre, the kilogram and the second: units that are the same for everyone. Today you will learn how those units were chosen, how to use the instruments that carry them, and where measuring stops being simple.
intro.art: A child and an adult each stretching a hand across the same table, with '9 spans' over the child and '6 spans' over the adult.

outcomes: I can give everyday examples where measuring is needed, such as buying goods, cooking, giving medicine and telling the time.
I can explain that measuring means comparing with a unit and counting, and that a measurement needs both a number and a unit.
I can name the standard units for length, mass, volume, time and temperature, and say why the whole world shares them.
I can choose a suitable instrument for a job and read it correctly.
I can explain why no measurement is perfectly exact, and why some things have no single true length.
I can estimate a length, a mass or a volume before I measure it.
I can say what measuring cannot tell us, and give one example.

explanations.concept: We measure when a guess is not good enough
explanations.definition: Measuring is finding out how much there is of something, as a number, so that different people can agree on it.
explanations.description: For many things a guess will do. You do not measure how far to step over a puddle. But think of the times a guess is not enough. A shopkeeper sells you rice, and both of you want to know it is one full kilogram. A nurse gives a baby medicine, and a little too much could harm. A train leaves at 6.15, not 'in the early evening'. A tailor cuts cloth that cannot be un-cut. In each case two people must agree, or a mistake would cost money, health or time. That is when people measure. Measuring turns 'a lot' and 'a little' into numbers that can be checked.
examples: Buying goods: 2 kilograms of onions, half a litre of milk, 3 metres of cloth, 5 litres of petrol.
Telling time: the school bell, a bus timetable, how long to boil an egg.
Cooking: one tumbler of rice to two tumblers of water.
Health: your height and weight on a clinic card, a fever of 101 degrees, 5 millilitres of cough syrup.
Building: a mason checks that a wall is straight and a door frame is 2 metres high.
explanations.one_view: That people measure in trade, cooking, health and timekeeping is plain to see in any home or market.
explanations.art: A market stall with a seller weighing onions on a balance, a wall clock behind, a tailor's tape hanging on a hook and a milk packet marked 500 mL.
explanations.context: This card gives the everyday reasons for measuring, before any units or instruments.

explanations.concept: Measuring is comparing with a unit and counting
explanations.definition: A unit is a fixed amount that we choose to compare other amounts with. A measurement is a number together with its unit.
explanations.description: To measure a table you pick something to compare it with, such as one hand span. That chosen amount is called a unit. Then you count how many units fit. If nine fit, the table is nine hand spans wide. Every measurement works this way, however clever the instrument. A ruler is a strip with the unit already marked many times, so that the counting is done for you. This means a measurement always has two parts: a number and a unit. '5' alone says nothing. Five what? Five centimetres is the width of a matchbox. Five kilometres is an hour's walk.
examples: 'The medicine dose is 5' could mean 5 drops or 5 spoonfuls. The unit decides.
A recipe that says 'add 2 of salt' cannot be followed.
A road sign says 'Madurai 40'. In India we know it means kilometres. A visitor from the United States, who is used to miles, might think the town much further away.
explanations.one_view: This is what the word measuring means in every science. The harder questions about it come in later cards.
explanations.art: A table with nine identical hand-span outlines laid end to end across it, numbered 1 to 9.
explanations.context: This card says what measuring is, and why a number without a unit means nothing.

explanations.concept: Body units came first, and they differ from person to person
explanations.definition: A body unit is a unit taken from part of the body, such as a finger width, a hand span, a forearm or a foot.
explanations.description: The first units were always at hand, because they were the hand. People measured cloth by the forearm, from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger. They measured a field by paces and a horse by hand widths. These units are quick, free and always with you. Their fault is plain. A tall weaver's forearm is longer than a short weaver's. Sell cloth by your own arm, and every sale is an argument. Body units work inside one family. They fail between strangers.
examples: A flower seller in Madurai still sells jasmine strings by the muzham, the length of the forearm.
The words foot and hand span are still in daily use, though few people measure with their feet.
A kolam is often set out in finger widths and hand spans, and it fits the doorstep of the person who draws it.

perspectives.who: Kautilya's Arthashastra, book 2, chapter 20, composed in India about 2,000 years ago
perspectives.explanation: The text sets out a ladder of lengths. Eight barley grains laid side by side make one angula, a finger width. Twenty-four angulas make one hasta, a forearm. By tying the finger to a count of grains, it tried to make a body unit the same for everyone.

perspectives.who: Craftspeople who build temples and homes by the old Indian texts on building
perspectives.explanation: Some traditions size a house from the owner's own forearm, so that the home fits the person who lives in it. For them a unit that differs from person to person is the purpose and not a fault.

explanations.art: Two weavers of different heights each measuring the same cloth along a forearm, with the cloth ending at different points on each arm.
explanations.context: This card shows where units began and why body units were not enough.

explanations.concept: Standard units are much older than the metre: the Harappan weights
explanations.definition: A standard unit is a unit that many people agree to keep exactly the same, by copying it from one shared example.
explanations.description: The cure for quarrelling over units is to make one unit and copy it for everyone. The cities of the Harappan people, who lived along the Indus and in Gujarat about 4,500 years ago, already did this. Archaeologists have found hundreds of small stone cubes there. They are weights for a balance. The smallest common one is a little under one gram. The next ones are 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 times as heavy, each double the one before. The same weights turn up in cities more than a thousand kilometres apart. Somebody was making sure that a trader in one city and a trader in another meant the same thing by one weight.
examples: At Lothal in Gujarat a piece of an ivory scale was found with marks about 1.7 millimetres apart, among the finest divisions known from that age.
Harappan bricks have the same proportions in city after city: the thickness, width and length are as 1 to 2 to 4.
The Arthashastra, book 2, chapter 19, tells the king's officer to have weights and measures checked and stamped at regular times, and to fine traders who use unstamped ones.

perspectives.who: Archaeologists such as Jonathan Mark Kenoyer
perspectives.explanation: The sameness of the weights across so wide a land shows shared rules of trade, and perhaps officers who checked them.

perspectives.who: Other archaeologists
perspectives.explanation: Nobody has read the Harappan writing, so we do not know who set the standard or how it was enforced. It may have been merchants' agreement and not a ruler's order.

explanations.art: A row of seven polished stone cubes in rising size beside a small two-pan balance, with '1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64' written under them.
explanations.context: This card shows that people in India made standard units thousands of years before the metric system.

explanations.concept: The metric system: one set of units for the whole world
explanations.definition: The metric system is a set of units, built on the metre, the kilogram and the second, in which larger and smaller units are made by multiplying or dividing by ten. Its modern form is called the International System of Units, or SI.
explanations.description: Until about 200 years ago every region had its own units. In the 1790s scientists in France designed a new system meant 'for all people, for all time'. They did not base it on a king's foot. They based the metre on the size of the Earth: one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator. They made every larger and smaller unit by tens, so that sums would be easy. Country after country joined. India changed over by a law passed in 1956, and the old seer, tola and gaz slowly left the shops. Today scientists in every country, and nearly all shops, use the same units.
examples: Before the change, a seer of rice was a little less than one kilogram, and its size was not exactly the same in every province.
A doctor in Kochi and a doctor in Brazil both write a dose in milligrams and mean the same amount.
The United States still uses miles, pounds and gallons in daily life. Its scientists use metric units.

perspectives.who: The French scientists of the 1790s, and scientists since
perspectives.explanation: One system, built on tens and open to all, removes cheating and mistakes and lets the whole world share its findings.

perspectives.who: People who keep older units, such as carpenters who work in inches and feet
perspectives.explanation: A foot divides neatly into halves, thirds and quarters, which ten does not. Old units grew out of real work and often suit the hand and the job.

explanations.art: An old brass seer weight and a wooden gaz stick on one side of a shop counter and a modern one-kilogram weight and a metre scale on the other.
explanations.context: This card tells how the world came to share one system of units, and when India joined.

explanations.concept: Kilo, centi and milli: one unit made big or small by tens
explanations.definition: A prefix is a short word put in front of a unit to make it larger or smaller. Kilo means one thousand, centi means one hundredth and milli means one thousandth.
explanations.description: In the metric system you do not need a new name for every size. You take one unit and put a prefix in front of it. Kilo means a thousand. So a kilometre is 1,000 metres and a kilogram is 1,000 grams. Centi means a hundredth. So 100 centimetres make one metre. Milli means a thousandth. So 1,000 millimetres make one metre, and 1,000 millilitres make one litre. Learn the three prefixes once, and they work for the metre, the gram and the litre alike. Changing from one size to another is only a matter of moving by tens.
examples: Your height may be 130 centimetres. That is 1.3 metres, or 1,300 millimetres.
A 500 millilitre packet of milk is half a litre.
A paracetamol tablet for a child may hold 250 milligrams of medicine, which is a quarter of a gram.
Mega means a million. A megawatt is a million watts.
explanations.one_view: The prefixes are fixed by international agreement and mean the same everywhere.
explanations.art: A ladder of steps labelled milli, centi, the plain unit, and kilo, with 'x10' arrows between the rungs.
explanations.context: This card explains the three prefixes that make sense of most labels on packets and rulers.

explanations.concept: Length: the metre and its instruments
explanations.definition: Length is how long something is from end to end. Its standard unit is the metre.
explanations.description: A metre is about the distance from the floor to the handle of a door. For small things we use centimetres and millimetres. For journeys we use kilometres. Each size of job has its own instrument. A 15 centimetre ruler suits a line in a notebook. A tailor's soft tape goes round a waist, which a stiff ruler cannot do. A steel tape that rolls into a case measures a room. A car counts kilometres by counting the turns of its wheels. The modern metre is no longer tied to the Earth. Since 1983 it has been defined as the distance light travels in a tiny, exactly stated fraction of a second.
examples: The thickness of a fingernail is about 1 millimetre. The width of a finger is about 1 centimetre.
A cricket pitch is 20.12 metres long.
By rail, Chennai is about 2,180 kilometres from New Delhi.
In 1865 and 1866 the surveyor Nain Singh Rawat measured the road to Lhasa by counting his own equal steps on a string of beads.
explanations.one_view: The unit of length and its definition are fixed by international agreement.
explanations.art: A notebook ruler, a tailor's soft tape and a steel roll-up tape laid side by side, each next to the thing it suits: a pencil line, a waist and a room.
explanations.context: This card covers the unit of length and which instrument fits which job.

explanations.concept: Mass: the kilogram, and what a balance really does
explanations.definition: Mass is the amount of matter in something. Its standard unit is the kilogram. A balance finds a mass by comparing it with known masses.
explanations.description: A one-litre bottle of water has a mass of about one kilogram. Small masses are given in grams: a paper clip is about one gram. The oldest instrument is the two-pan balance. You put the vegetables on one pan and metal weights on the other. When the beam is level, the two sides match. A balance never tells you a mass directly. It only says 'these two are equal'. A digital kitchen scale works differently. It measures how hard the thing presses down, and shows the answer in grams. What matter finally is, scientists cannot yet say. The mass of everyday things turns out to come mostly from energy held inside the centres of atoms.
examples: A newborn baby is usually about 3 kilograms.
A cooking gas cylinder holds 14.2 kilograms of gas.
Gold is still often spoken of in tolas. One tola is about 11.7 grams. Jewellers' bills today are in grams.
A letter is weighed in grams at the post office, and a lorry in tonnes at a weighbridge. A tonne is 1,000 kilograms.
explanations.one_view: The unit of mass and how balances work are agreed. The open question of what matter is belongs to another lesson and is listed among the open questions.
explanations.art: A two-pan balance with tomatoes on one pan and a one-kilogram iron weight on the other, the beam level, beside a digital kitchen scale showing 1000 g.
explanations.context: This card covers the unit of mass and shows that a balance works by matching.

explanations.concept: Volume: litres and millilitres, and how to measure a stone
explanations.definition: Volume is the amount of space something takes up. For liquids the usual units are the litre and the millilitre.
explanations.description: A litre is the space inside a cube that is 10 centimetres along each edge. A millilitre is the space inside a cube one centimetre along each edge. One teaspoon holds about 5 millilitres. Liquids are measured in a jug or a narrow tube with marks on the side, called a measuring cylinder. The makers of the metric system tied its units together neatly: one litre of water has a mass of one kilogram. What about the volume of a stone, which has no neat edges? Lower the stone into a measuring jug of water. The water level rises. The rise is exactly the volume of the stone.
examples: A milk packet is 500 millilitres. A bucket holds about 15 litres.
The cap of a cough syrup bottle is marked at 5 and 10 millilitres, because a kitchen spoon is not a reliable measure for medicine.
A tall thin tumbler and a short wide bowl can hold exactly the same volume, though the tumbler looks as if it holds more.
Grain was long sold by volume in India, in measures such as the padi in Tamil Nadu and the nazhi and para in Kerala.
explanations.one_view: The units of volume, and finding a volume by the rise of water, are agreed and easy to check at home.
explanations.art: A measuring jug with water at the 300 mL mark, and the same jug with a stone lowered in and the water at 350 mL, with '50 mL' marked between.
explanations.context: This card covers the units of volume and a way to measure the volume of an odd-shaped thing.

explanations.concept: Time: the second, and clocks from a sinking bowl to an atom
explanations.definition: The standard unit of time is the second. A clock is anything that repeats in a steady way and can be counted.
explanations.description: To measure time you need something that repeats steadily: a swing, a drip, a shadow going round. Old India used a copper bowl with a small hole, floated on water. The bowl filled slowly and sank in exactly one ghati, which is 24 minutes. Sixty ghatis made a day and a night. We divide an hour into 60 minutes because the people of ancient Babylon, more than 3,500 years ago, counted in sixties. Today the second is defined by an atom. A caesium atom gives off waves that repeat 9,192,631,770 times in one second, and atomic clocks count them. Clocks measure time very well. What time itself is has no agreed answer in science.
examples: At the Jantar Mantar in Jaipur, built about 1730, a sundial 27 metres tall throws a shadow that moves about one millimetre every second. It can be read to about two seconds.
India's official time is kept by atomic clocks at the National Physical Laboratory in New Delhi.
Your pulse is a rough clock, beating about 80 to 100 times a minute when you sit quietly.
The Chinese pilgrim Yijing wrote in the 7th century CE that the monks at Nalanda kept the hours with a sinking bowl and struck a drum each time the bowl went down.

perspectives.who: The Surya Siddhanta, an Indian text on astronomy, chapter 13
perspectives.explanation: It describes the copper bowl with a hole that sinks sixty times in a day and a night, and treats time as something counted by the turning of the sky.

perspectives.who: Isaac Newton, in 1687
perspectives.explanation: He held that time flows evenly by itself, the same everywhere, whether or not any clock is counting.

perspectives.who: Albert Einstein in 1905, and physicists since
perspectives.explanation: They showed that clocks moving at different speeds, or at different heights, run at different rates. So there is no single time for everyone. Some physicists, such as Carlo Rovelli, think time may not be a basic part of nature at all.

explanations.art: A copper bowl half sunk in a basin of water on the left, the great triangular sundial at Jaipur in the middle and a small box labelled 'atomic clock' on the right.
explanations.context: This card covers the unit of time, India's old clocks, and the fact that nobody can yet say what time is.

explanations.concept: Temperature: degrees Celsius, and a scale that people chose
explanations.definition: Temperature tells how hot or cold something is. The everyday unit is the degree Celsius, on a scale where water freezes at 0 and boils at 100.
explanations.description: A thermometer measures temperature. On the Celsius scale, ice melts at 0 degrees and water boils at 100 degrees at sea level. These two marks were chosen by people. When the Swedish scientist Anders Celsius made his scale in 1742, he put 100 at freezing and 0 at boiling. It was turned the other way round after his death. Fever thermometers in India often show another scale, called Fahrenheit, on which a healthy body is about 98.6 degrees. That is the same warmth as about 37 degrees Celsius. One temperature can have two numbers, and nothing about the body has changed.
examples: A fever thermometer covers only about 35 to 42 degrees Celsius, in small steps, because that is all a body needs.
A laboratory thermometer covers about minus 10 to 110 degrees Celsius, in larger steps.
A hot summer afternoon in Nagpur can reach 45 degrees Celsius. A winter night in Leh can fall to minus 15.
Scientists also use the kelvin scale, which starts at the coldest temperature there can be, about minus 273 degrees Celsius.
explanations.one_view: The temperature scales are fixed by agreement and can be converted exactly into each other.
explanations.art: A fever thermometer and a long laboratory thermometer side by side, with the fever thermometer's short range marked as a small band on the long one.
explanations.context: This card covers the unit of temperature and shows that the numbers on a scale were chosen by people.

explanations.concept: Choosing an instrument: how much can it measure, and how finely?
explanations.definition: The range of an instrument is the smallest and largest amount it can measure. Its smallest division is the smallest step marked on it.
explanations.description: Before you measure, ask two questions about the instrument. First, what is its range? A bathroom scale can weigh a person but not a lorry. Second, what is its smallest division? A bathroom scale shows steps of 100 grams, so it cannot weigh a letter of 20 grams. A kitchen scale shows steps of 1 gram, and it can. Pick an instrument whose range covers your thing and whose smallest step is much smaller than your thing. There is also a trick for things too small for your instrument. Measure many of them together and divide.
examples: One sheet of paper is too thin for a ruler. A pile of 100 sheets is about 1 centimetre thick. So one sheet is about one-hundredth of a centimetre, which is one-tenth of a millimetre.
To find the mass of one grain of rice on a kitchen scale, weigh 100 grains and divide by 100.
A jeweller's balance reads to one-thousandth of a gram and is kept inside a glass case, because a breath of air would disturb it.
explanations.one_view: Range and smallest division are plain features printed on every instrument.
explanations.art: A bathroom scale with a letter on it showing 0.0, beside a kitchen scale with the same letter showing 20 g.
explanations.context: This card teaches how to pick the right instrument, and a way to measure something too small for it.

explanations.concept: Reading an instrument: start at zero and look straight on
explanations.definition: A reading is the number you take from an instrument. To read correctly, the instrument must start from zero and your eye must be directly in line with the mark.
explanations.description: Three habits prevent most wrong readings. First, check the zero. On many rulers the zero mark is a little way in from the end, so line up the mark and not the end. A kitchen scale must show 0 before you put anything on it. Second, look straight on. If you read a ruler or a jug from one side, the mark seems to shift. Bring your eye level with the mark. Third, in a jug or tube, water curves up a little at the edges. Read the flat bottom of the curve, with the jug standing on a level table.
examples: Hold a pencil upright a little in front of a ruler and look with one eye, then the other. The pencil seems to jump along the ruler.
Two children read the same jug as 240 and 260 millilitres because one looked from above and one from below.
A shopkeeper presses the 'tare' button with the empty bowl on the scale, so that the scale shows 0 and weighs only what goes into the bowl.
explanations.one_view: These are working rules that every laboratory teaches, and there is nothing in them to dispute.
explanations.art: A measuring cylinder with three eyes drawn at different heights, sight lines to the water level, and only the level sight line reading the true mark.
explanations.context: This card gives the three habits for reading a ruler, a scale and a jug correctly.

explanations.concept: Estimating: a sensible guess before you measure
explanations.definition: An estimate is a careful guess at an amount, made by comparing it with something whose size you already know.
explanations.description: Good measurers guess first. An estimate before you measure does two jobs. It helps you pick the right instrument. It also catches mistakes: if you guess 'about one metre' and your tape says 10, you look again. To estimate well you need a few sizes that you carry with you. Your finger is about 1 centimetre wide. A door is about 2 metres high. A teaspoon holds 5 millilitres. A full one-litre bottle has a mass of 1 kilogram. With these, most everyday things can be guessed to within about a quarter of their true size.
examples: A vegetable seller can put very nearly one kilogram of tomatoes on the pan by feel before the balance checks it.
A cook adds salt 'by eye' and gets close to the same amount each day.
The physicist Enrico Fermi was known for working out rough answers to big questions from a few known sizes, such as how many piano tuners work in a city.
explanations.one_view: Estimating is a skill, and its use before measuring is taught by scientists and engineers everywhere.
explanations.art: A child holding a finger against a pencil to guess its length, with a thought bubble showing '1 cm' on the finger and '15?' above the pencil.
explanations.context: This card shows why a guess comes before a measurement, and gives sizes to carry in your head.

explanations.concept: Some things have no single true length: India's coast
explanations.definition: The measured length of a very wiggly line, such as a coast, depends on the size of the step used to measure it. A smaller step follows more bends and gives a longer answer.
explanations.description: For many years India's coast was listed as about 7,516 kilometres. A few years ago the government measured again and gave about 11,098 kilometres. The sea had not moved. The new survey used maps showing far more detail, so the measuring line went in and out of many more bays and creeks. A coast is jagged at every size. Measure it with steps of 100 kilometres and you skip most of the bends. Measure with steps of one kilometre and you follow more. Measure round every rock and the number rises again. So asking for 'the length of the coast' is not enough. You must also say how fine the measuring was.
examples: Lay a thread loosely along the edge of a torn chapati, then measure the same edge with a stiff ruler in straight steps. The thread gives the longer answer.
The length of a smooth thing, such as the edge of a steel plate, hardly changes when you use a finer ruler. The puzzle belongs to jagged things.
A river's length and the edge of a banyan leaf behave like the coast.

perspectives.who: Lewis Fry Richardson, an English scientist, in work printed in 1961
perspectives.explanation: He noticed that neighbouring countries gave different lengths for the border they shared. He found that the smaller the measuring step, the longer the border came out, in a regular way.

perspectives.who: Benoit Mandelbrot, in 1967, in a paper titled 'How long is the coast of Britain?'
perspectives.explanation: He showed that shapes like coasts keep their roughness however closely you look. He later named such shapes fractals and gave a number for how rough each one is.

perspectives.who: Surveyors and governments
perspectives.explanation: For law and planning one number is needed. So they agree on a map scale and a method, and state it. The number is then a fair answer to a clearly stated question.

explanations.art: The same stretch of jagged coast three times, measured with a few long straight steps, with more medium steps and with many tiny steps, with the total length written under each and growing.
explanations.context: This card pushes against the belief that every thing has one true size waiting to be read.

explanations.concept: Units now rest on nature's constants: the kilogram left its vault in 2019
explanations.definition: Since 2019 every standard unit has been defined from a constant of nature, which is a number that is found to be the same everywhere and at all times.
explanations.description: From 1889 the kilogram was a real object: a small cylinder of metal locked in a vault near Paris. Every country had a copy. India's is copy number 57, kept in New Delhi. There was a weakness. Over a hundred years the cylinder and its copies drifted apart by about 50 millionths of a gram, and nobody could say which had changed. An object can be scratched, lose atoms or be lost. So in 2019 the countries of the world agreed to define the kilogram from a fixed number of nature called the Planck constant. The metre was already tied to the speed of light, and the second to the caesium atom. Now any laboratory with the right equipment can make the units afresh.
examples: The shopkeeper's one-kilogram weight is checked against an inspector's weight, which was checked against a state laboratory's, which was checked against the national one. This chain of checks is how your kilogram of rice is tied to the world's kilogram.
In India, weights and scales used for selling must carry an inspector's stamp, under the Legal Metrology Act of 2009.
explanations.one_view: The definitions were agreed by the member countries of the metre treaty in 2018 and took effect on 20 May 2019.
explanations.art: A small shiny metal cylinder under three glass covers on the left, crossed by an arrow leading to a drawing of a balance with a coil of wire and a beam of light on the right.
explanations.context: This card tells how the units stopped depending on objects, and how a shop's weight is linked to the world's.

explanations.concept: Mixing up units can be costly
explanations.definition: A unit error happens when a number is passed on without its unit, or with the wrong one, and is then used as if it were in a different unit.
explanations.description: In September 1999 a spacecraft called Mars Climate Orbiter reached Mars after a journey of more than nine months. It flew too low and was destroyed in the planet's air. The cause was found within weeks. One team had sent numbers for the pushes of the craft's small engines in an old American unit. The other team's computer read the same numbers as metric units. Nobody had checked the unit. The spacecraft had cost about 125 million dollars. The numbers were all correct. Only the units were missing.
examples: In 1983 a passenger aeroplane in Canada ran out of fuel in mid-air because the fuel had been worked out in pounds when the new aircraft needed kilograms. The pilots glided it to a safe landing on an old airfield at Gimli.
A parent told 'give 5' of a medicine may give 5 millilitres or 5 spoonfuls. Doctors now ask that doses for children be written in millilitres only.
Land in India is still sold by the bigha in many states. A bigha in one state can be about twice as large as a bigha in another.
explanations.one_view: These events were investigated and their causes are on public record.
explanations.art: A small spacecraft heading too low towards a red planet, with two speech bubbles from two control rooms, one showing a number with 'pounds' and one showing the same number with 'newtons'.
explanations.context: This card shows, with real events, why the unit matters as much as the number.

explanations.concept: Measuring what you cannot reach: the Earth and Mount Everest
explanations.definition: An indirect measurement finds a size by measuring other things that can be reached, such as angles and shadows, and calculating.
explanations.description: Nobody has stretched a tape round the Earth or stood a ruler beside Everest. Such sizes are worked out. About 240 BCE, Eratosthenes, who kept the great library at Alexandria in Egypt, heard that at noon on midsummer day the Sun shone straight down a well in the town of Syene. In Alexandria, on the same day, a pillar threw a short shadow. From the angle of that shadow and the distance between the two towns he worked out the distance round the whole Earth, and came close to the true value of about 40,000 kilometres. In 1852 Radhanath Sikdar, a mathematician from Bengal working for the Survey of India, calculated from angles measured far away that a Himalayan peak was the highest known in the world. It was later named Mount Everest, after a British surveyor.
examples: The height first announced for the peak was 29,002 feet, about 8,840 metres. The figure agreed by Nepal and China in 2020 is 8,848.86 metres.
You can find how tall a tree stands by measuring the shadow of the tree and the shadow of a metre stick at the same moment.
Aryabhata, in 499 CE, gave the Earth's width as 1,050 yojanas. Scholars do not agree on the length of his yojana, so they do not agree on how close he came.

perspectives.who: Many Indian writers
perspectives.explanation: They hold that Sikdar found the highest peak and that naming it after George Everest, who never saw it, wiped out his credit.

perspectives.who: Some historians of the Survey of India
perspectives.explanation: They point out that the calculation was the work of a team over several years. The records do not show clearly how much of the final result was Sikdar's alone.

explanations.art: A well with sunlight going straight down on one side, a pillar with a short shadow on the other, and a curved line of the Earth joining them with the angle marked.
explanations.context: This card shows how people measured things far too large to reach, and names the Indian mathematician behind Everest's height.

explanations.concept: Other living beings measure too
explanations.definition: Many living beings sense amounts such as distance, length of night and number of touches, and act on them.
explanations.description: Measuring did not begin with people. A desert ant in the Sahara walks a winding path to find food and then runs home in a straight line. How do they know the distance? In 2006 scientists glued tiny stilts to some ants' legs after the ants reached the food. With longer legs and longer steps, those ants ran too far and passed their nest. Ants whose legs were made shorter stopped too soon. The ants had been keeping count of their steps. Plants measure as well. Many flower only when the nights reach a certain length. A Venus flytrap shuts only after two touches on the hairs inside within about half a minute.
examples: Chrysanthemum plants flower when the nights grow long. Growers keep lamps on at night to hold them back until the flowers are wanted.
A rice plant of a traditional variety senses the shortening days and flowers at the right week of the season.
Your own body keeps a clock of about 24 hours, which is why you feel sleepy at nearly the same time each night.

perspectives.who: Matthias Wittlinger, Rüdiger Wehner and Harald Wolf, who did the ant test in 2006
perspectives.explanation: They describe the ant as having a step counter, a body mechanism that adds up strides.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study animal and plant minds
perspectives.explanation: The ant senses, remembers and decides when to stop and search. A plant counting touches is also keeping a memory. Some scientists call these automatic mechanisms. What it is like for the ant, nobody knows.

perspectives.who: W. W. Garner and H. A. Allard, American plant scientists, in 1920
perspectives.explanation: They found that tobacco and soya plants flower according to the length of day and night, and showed that a plant keeps track of time.

explanations.art: Three desert ants on sand heading to a nest hole: one with normal legs stopping at the hole, one on stilts running past it and one with short legs stopping before it.
explanations.context: This card shows that ants and plants measure, with the experiment that proved it for ants.

explanations.concept: Everyday measuring in India: what to read on a packet and at a pump
explanations.definition: The law in India requires that goods sold by measure are measured with checked instruments, and that packets state how much they hold.
explanations.description: You can use this lesson every time you shop. Every packet must print its net quantity, which is how much is inside without the wrapping: 500 g, 1 L, 200 mL. A petrol pump must show zero before it starts and shows the litres as they flow. A shop's scale must carry an inspector's seal. Alongside the metric units, older ones live on. Height is spoken in feet and inches. Cloth is sometimes sold by the yard. Land is sold by the cent in Kerala and Tamil Nadu, the guntha in Maharashtra and the bigha in the north. Knowing which unit is being used, and asking when you are not sure, is part of measuring well.
examples: A biscuit packet may look large and hold only 60 grams. Compare the price for each 100 grams, not the size of the packet.
A clinic card records a child's height in centimetres and weight in kilograms at every visit, to see how the child is growing.
The India Meteorological Department measures rain in millimetres: the depth the water would have if it stayed on flat ground.
An auto-rickshaw meter measures both the distance travelled and the time spent waiting.
explanations.one_view: These are rules and customs that anyone can check in a shop.
explanations.art: A close-up of a food packet with a finger pointing at 'Net quantity 500 g', beside a petrol pump display showing 0.00 litres.
explanations.context: This card brings the units into the market, the clinic and the street.

explanations.concept: Can everything be measured?
explanations.definition: People disagree about whether everything real can be given a number, and about what is lost when something is turned into a number.
explanations.description: Measuring is so useful that it is easy to think that only what is measured is real. A doctor asks, 'How bad is the pain, from 0 to 10?' You say 6. Your friend with the same injury says 3. Has the doctor measured pain? There is no unit of pain to compare with and no instrument. The same trouble comes up with happiness, cleverness, beauty and kindness. Some scientists say that these will be measured one day, as temperature finally was. Others say that some things are known in other ways, by watching, by listening and by living with them. Science itself began as careful thinking about nature. Measuring is one of its tools.
examples: Before thermometers, hot and cold were only feelings. It took about 200 years of work to make temperature a number that everyone agreed on.
A school mark turns a term of learning into one number. Ask what the number shows and what it leaves out.
Putting a cold thermometer into a small cup of warm water cools the water a little. The act of measuring can change the thing measured.

perspectives.who: William Thomson, Lord Kelvin, in a lecture of 1883
perspectives.explanation: He said that when you can measure what you are speaking about and express it in numbers, you have real knowledge of it. When you cannot, your knowledge is of a thin and unsatisfying kind.

perspectives.who: William Bruce Cameron, an American sociologist, in 1963
perspectives.explanation: He wrote that not everything that can be counted counts, and not everything that counts can be counted.

perspectives.who: Jain philosophers, in the Tattvartha Sutra 1.6, by Umasvati, about the 2nd to 5th century CE
perspectives.explanation: The text says that knowledge comes through full means of knowing and also through partial standpoints. Any one way of knowing a thing, a measurement included, gives one side of it.

explanations.art: A doctor holding a card with a row of faces from smiling to crying numbered 0 to 10, and two children pointing at different faces.
explanations.context: This card asks where measuring reaches its limit, with views on both sides.

agreed.text: The first metre was very slightly too short, and it was kept anyway.
agreed.evidence: The French survey of the 1790s assumed a slightly wrong shape for the Earth. Later, better measurements showed that the metre bar was about one-fifth of a millimetre shorter than one ten-millionth of the distance from pole to equator. By then the bar was in use, so the bar stayed the metre. This shows that a unit is an agreement.

agreed.text: Two very exact clocks at different heights tick at different rates.
agreed.evidence: In 2010 James Chin-Wen Chou and his colleagues in the United States raised one of two atomic clocks by about 33 centimetres. The higher clock ran faster by a tiny, measurable amount, as Einstein's theory of gravity predicts.

agreed.text: People's eyes are easily fooled about length, which is one reason instruments are needed.
agreed.evidence: In the drawing published by Franz Müller-Lyer in 1889, two equal lines look unequal because of the arrow-heads at their ends. Nearly everyone sees the illusion, and a ruler settles it at once.

agreed.text: Human bodies have not always measured about 37 degrees Celsius.
agreed.evidence: In 2020 Myroslava Protsiv, Julie Parsonnet and their colleagues compared temperature records of people in the United States from the 1860s to 2017. The average body temperature had fallen by about half a degree Celsius. A 'normal' value turns out to be a measurement of certain people at a certain time.

challenging.claim: If you cannot measure something, your knowledge of it is poor.
challenging.who: Lord Kelvin in 1883, and many scientists since
challenging.for: Sciences leapt forward each time something vague became a number: temperature, electric current, the age of rocks. Numbers can be checked by strangers, and opinions cannot.
challenging.against: A field naturalist such as Jane Goodall learnt what chimpanzees are like by years of patient watching, before any numbers. Much of what we know about one another, and about other beings, is of this kind. A number can also give false confidence.
challenging.context: This is the most famous claim for measuring. Scientists themselves disagree about how far it goes.

challenging.claim: Intelligence can be measured with a single number.
challenging.who: Charles Spearman in 1904, and makers of IQ tests since
challenging.for: People who do well on one kind of thinking test tend to do well on others. Test scores predict school results fairly well.
challenging.against: In 1981 the biologist Stephen Jay Gould argued that a pattern in test scores had been mistaken for a real thing inside the head. Howard Gardner in 1983 proposed many kinds of intelligence. Tests have also been unfair to people of other languages and cultures, and say nothing about the minds of other beings.
challenging.context: This shows what can go wrong when something is measured before anyone agrees what it is.

challenging.claim: The whole world should give up every old unit and use only metric ones.
challenging.who: The international metre treaty of 1875 and most scientists
challenging.for: One system prevents costly mistakes, cheating and confusion, and lets all people share knowledge.
challenging.against: Old units carry the knowledge of crafts and places. A carpenter's inches divide easily into halves and quarters. A unit such as the muzham needs no instrument. Some people ask why working customs should vanish to suit laboratories.
challenging.context: Both sides agree that science needs one system. They disagree about daily life.

challenging.claim: Measuring always disturbs what is measured, so we can never know a thing as it is.
challenging.who: A popular reading of Werner Heisenberg's work of 1927
challenging.for: For the very smallest particles, measuring one feature exactly does leave another feature unsettled. A thermometer does change the temperature of a small drop.
challenging.against: For everyday things the disturbance can be made far too small to matter: a ruler does not change a table. Physicists also point out that Heisenberg's finding is about what particles are like, not about clumsy instruments. In physics an 'observer' is any measuring device and not a mind.
challenging.context: This claim stretches a real finding of physics further than physicists do. It is here so that the real finding and the stretch can be told apart.

big_questions.q: Your hand gave the table one width and a grown-up's hand gave another. Does the table have a width when nobody is measuring it?
big_questions.hint: Ask what would be left of the word 'width' if there were nothing at all to compare the table with.

big_questions.q: India's coast is 7,516 kilometres by one count and 11,098 by another. Is there a true length that both are trying to reach?
big_questions.hint: Imagine measuring round every pebble, then every grain of sand. What happens to the number?

big_questions.q: For 130 years the kilogram was one metal cylinder. If that cylinder lost a speck, did it become lighter, or did everything else in the world become heavier?
big_questions.hint: Ask what 'one kilogram' meant during those years, and what you would have to compare the cylinder with to find out.

big_questions.q: A water clock is checked against a watch, and a watch against an atomic clock. What is the atomic clock checked against?
big_questions.hint: Think about what people do when they have two of the best clocks and they disagree.

big_questions.q: Can you measure how much someone loves you? If you cannot, is the love less real than the width of a table?
big_questions.hint: Think about how you do know such a thing, and whether a number would add anything.

big_questions.q: People chose the metre, the kilogram and the second. Would visitors from another world have the same units? Would they have the same answers?
big_questions.hint: Separate what is chosen, such as the size of the unit, from what is found, such as how many times one thing fits into another.

big_questions.q: A school mark turns months of your learning into one number. What does that number show, and what does it leave out?
big_questions.hint: List three things you learnt this year that no test asked about.

big_questions.q: A desert ant counts steps and a plant measures the night. Is that the same thing you do with a ruler?
big_questions.hint: Compare what each of you does with the result. Then ask what a unit is for the ant.

big_questions.q: Trade needs measures that everyone trusts. Is a measurement a fact about the thing, or an agreement between people?
big_questions.hint: Think about the kilogram of tomatoes. Which part would stay the same if every person vanished, and which part would not?

story.title: The Kilogram Nobody Could Weigh
story.note: A made-up story set in Delhi. The children, the vegetable seller and the scientist are imagined. What is real: from 1889 to 2019 the kilogram was a metal cylinder kept in a vault near Paris. India holds copy number 57 at the National Physical Laboratory in New Delhi. Over about a century the cylinder and its copies drifted apart by about 50 millionths of a gram. Since 20 May 2019 the kilogram has been defined from the Planck constant. The kilogram was first chosen in the 1790s as the mass of one litre of water.
text: At the Saturday market, Kamla didi put a kilo of tomatoes on one pan of her balance and an iron weight on the other. The beam swung and settled level.
Kabir, who was ten and liked an argument, pointed at the iron weight. 'How do we know that is really one kilo?'
Kamla didi was not offended. She turned the weight over. A small seal was pressed into the bottom. 'The inspector checks it against his own weights and stamps it. No stamp, and I pay a fine.'
'And who checks the inspector's weights?'

'Ask her mother,' said Kamla didi, nodding at Zoya. Zoya, who was also ten, had come with Kabir to carry the bags. Her mother Nasreen worked at the National Physical Laboratory, where India's measures are kept.

That evening Nasreen drew a chain of boxes on the back of an envelope. Kamla's weight. The inspector's weight. The state laboratory's. The national laboratory's. 'And until 2019,' she said, 'the chain ended here.' She drew a small cylinder under three glass covers. 'One piece of metal, locked in a vault near Paris since 1889. That cylinder was the kilogram. India has copy number fifty-seven. I have seen it.'
'Who checked the one in Paris?' said Kabir.

'Nobody could. That was the trouble. Every forty years or so, the copies were carried to Paris and compared with it. Over a hundred years they drifted apart, by about fifty millionths of a gram. That is roughly what a fingerprint weighs.'
'So the Paris one got lighter,' said Zoya.

'Or the copies got heavier. Or both. There was no way to tell, because the cylinder was the kilogram, by definition. If it lost a speck of metal, it was still exactly one kilogram. The rule said so. Which meant that everything else in the universe had become a tiny bit heavier.'
Kabir laughed. Then he stopped. 'That is silly. But the rule does say it.'
'You two became heavier as well,' said Nasreen, 'without eating anything.'

Zoya was thinking about the two pans. 'A balance never tells you how heavy a thing is,' she said slowly. 'It only tells you that two things match. Kamla didi's weight matches the inspector's. His matches the next one. It is matching, all the way up. And the top one had nothing to match with.'

'So in 2019 the countries changed the top of the chain,' said Nasreen. 'Now the kilogram is tied to a number of nature called the Planck constant. It is part of how light and atoms behave, and as far as anyone can tell it is the same everywhere. A laboratory can build a special balance that matches the Earth's pull on a mass against an electric push worked out from that number. Any country can build one. Nothing is locked in a vault.'
'So now it is the true kilogram at last,' said Kabir.

'It is a kilogram that everybody can check,' said Nasreen. 'Is that the same as true? People chose its size, in the 1790s. They took the mass of one litre of water. It could have been any size. Nature did not hand it to us.'
The next Saturday, Kabir told Kamla didi the whole story. She listened while she weighed brinjals.
'In my grandmother's village she sold by the handful,' she said. 'No weights and no stamp. People bought from her because her handful was honest.'
'A handful cannot be checked,' said Kabir.
'It was checked every day,' said Kamla didi, 'by everyone who came back.'

Zoya watched the pans swing and settle. Tomatoes on one side and iron on the other, two things as different as could be, and the beam said only: these match. She tried to think of one thing, anywhere, that could be measured with nothing set beside it. She could not.
story.epiphany: Every weighing was a matching, from the market stall up to the vault in Paris, and the top of the chain had nothing to be matched with. A measurement turned out to rest on comparison and on trust: the stamp on a weight, a number of nature, or the buyers who came back.
ask: Zoya said a balance only tells you that two things match. Is there any instrument that does more than that?
Nasreen asked if a kilogram that everybody can check is the same as a true kilogram. What do you think?
Kamla didi's grandmother was checked by the people who came back. Is that a kind of measuring?
Can you think of one thing that could be measured with nothing beside it?

how_we_found_out.story: Before the 1790s, people held that each town's own measures were good enough. It was believable, because most buying and selling happened between neighbours. In France alone, historians count about 250,000 different local units, and the same name often meant different amounts in the next valley. Traders and tax collectors could cheat, and scientists could not compare results. In 1791 the French Academy of Sciences proposed a unit taken from the Earth itself, so that it would belong to no king. From 1792 to 1798 two astronomers, Jean-Baptiste Delambre and Pierre Méchain, measured the land from Dunkirk in the north to Barcelona in the south, through a revolution and a war, and were arrested more than once as spies. Méchain found that some of his readings near Barcelona did not agree with each other. He hid this and it troubled him for the rest of his life. From their survey a platinum metre bar was made in 1799. In 1875 seventeen countries signed a treaty to share the metre and the kilogram. India joined in 1957. In 1983 the metre was tied to the speed of light, and in 2019 the kilogram was tied to a constant of nature.
how_we_found_out.who: Jean-Baptiste Delambre, Pierre Méchain, the French Academy of Sciences, and the countries of the metre treaty
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People held that every place could keep its own units without harm. It fitted a world where goods and ideas did not travel far. As trade and science crossed borders, the confusion and cheating showed that shared units were needed.

roots.context: You have learnt how to measure and how units were agreed. Now we ask what measuring tells us about ourselves, about life and about this world.

deep_truth.truth: You measured a torn edge with big steps and then with small steps, and the small steps gave a longer answer. India's coast did the same: 7,516 kilometres by one survey and 11,098 by a finer one. The edge did not change between the two counts. Each smaller step follows more bends, so the answer keeps growing. So 'how long is it?' has no final answer until we also say how fine the steps were.
deep_truth.habit: We treat 'how long is it?' as a complete question, with one answer waiting inside the thing. For a jagged edge the question is unfinished until the size of the step is named.
deep_truth.evidence: In the wiggly line test the same torn edge came out longer each time the step got smaller. For example, a child might get about 18 centimetres with 3 centimetre steps and about 24 with 1 centimetre steps: your numbers will differ. Put your own two numbers here.

three.who_am_i: Each number about you, your height, your weight, your marks, is a meeting between you and a chosen way of measuring. Change the way and the number changes, while you stay as you are. Understanding this, you need not mistake any number for yourself.
three.what_is_life: An ant counts steps and a plant measures the night. Every living being measures what matters to them, with their own body as the instrument. To be alive is, in part, to be a measurer of the world.
three.what_is_this_world: A coast has no single length and a kilogram is an agreement tied to a constant of nature. The world gives the same answers to everyone who asks the same question in the same way. It does not give answers to questions nobody has asked.

roots.thread: This lesson treated measuring as comparing. Then it found a case where the answer depends on the fineness of the comparison, and never settles. That is a measured fact about coasts. It suggests that a measurement is something that happens between a measurer and a thing, and is not found in either one alone. Consciousness is the ground in which the measurer and the measured both arise, and measuring is one way that ground meets itself. This last step is not science. Quantum physics, where measuring also matters deeply, does not prove it either: in physics an 'observer' is any measuring device and not a mind. Many scientists stop at the measured fact, and their view is given below.

teachings.teaching: That is whole, and this is whole. From the whole, the whole comes out. When the whole is taken from the whole, the whole still remains.
teachings.link: Every measurement in this lesson works by taking away and counting: so many units, with some left over. The verse speaks of something for which taking away changes nothing. It marks a place where measuring, by its own method, cannot go.

teachings.teaching: That which the mind cannot think, but by which the mind thinks: know that alone to be Brahman, the one ground, and not what people take it to be.
teachings.link: The lesson found that every measurement needs a measurer. The sage points at what does the knowing and says it cannot be made into a thing known. Science has not found a way to measure the one who measures, which is the open question of consciousness.

teachings.source: Protagoras of Abdera, about 450 BCE, as reported in Plato's 'Theaetetus', section 152a
teachings.teaching: He said that the human being is the measure of all things.
teachings.link: The coast finding gives him a point: the answer does depend on the measurer. This lesson also shows where he stops short. The ant and the plant are measures too, each of their own world.

science.text: The measured length of a coast grows as the measuring step shrinks. This has been confirmed on many coasts and borders since Richardson's work was printed in 1961.
Many physicists think there is a smallest length that has any meaning, called the Planck length, far smaller than an atom. No experiment has reached it.

other_view.who: Scientific realists, and the Nyaya school of Indian philosophy
other_view.view: Things have their sizes whether or not anyone measures them. A stone has a mass and a steel plate has a width, and careful measurers close in on the same value. The coast is a special case of a jagged shape, and even there, once the step size is stated, everyone gets the same answer. Measuring finds what is there. It does not help to make it.

practice.title: Your own breath as a unit
practice.say: Sit comfortably and close your eyes. Breathe in and out slowly, and count ten breaths. That was a length of time, measured in your own unit. Now open your eyes and look at something far away, then something near. Before you reach for any number, notice that you already know which is further. Sit for three more breaths with that knowing.
practice.kid: Close your eyes and count ten slow breaths. You have just measured time with your own unit. Open your eyes and look at something far and something near. Notice that you know which is further without any number. Take three more breaths.

ask: Your wiggly edge had two lengths. Which one was its real length, and why?
If your height is a meeting between you and a tape, where is 'your height' when the tape is put away?
What do you know for certain about someone you love that you have never measured?
roots.art: A child kneeling over a torn paper edge with a short and a long strip of card for measuring steps, and two different totals written beside the edge.

open_questions.q: Is there a smallest possible length and a shortest possible time?
open_questions.why_open: Some theories that try to join gravity with the physics of tiny particles say that space and time come in smallest pieces. Those pieces would be far too small for any instrument that exists, so the idea cannot yet be tested.

Clocks measure time to astonishing exactness, and physics uses it in every sum. There is still no agreed account of what time is, or of why it seems to flow one way. Some physicists think it is not a basic part of nature.

open_questions.q: Are the constants of nature truly constant?
open_questions.why_open: The units now rest on numbers such as the speed of light and the Planck constant. Astronomers compare light from very distant, very old galaxies with light made in laboratories to see if these numbers have changed. So far no change has been confirmed, but the search goes on.

open_questions.q: Can experiences such as pain be measured?
open_questions.why_open: Brain scans show activity that goes with pain, and people can rate their pain from 0 to 10. Nobody has shown how to compare one being's pain with another's, because there is no unit and no way to set two experiences side by side.

open_questions.q: What is matter, and where does mass come from?
open_questions.why_open: Most of the mass of everyday things comes from energy holding together the particles inside the centres of atoms. What matter finally is, and why the basic particles have the masses they have, is not known.

playtest: Untried parts: no part of this lesson has been done in a real home yet. The bottle clock test (e1), the sinking-cup clock (ch2) and the wiggly line test (a1) were worked out from how water flows and how steps add up, and they all depend on a step where the family tunes or repeats until the result shows. In e1, a first-minute fall of 1 to 1.5 centimetres from a 12 centimetre line should mean a 16 to 24 minute emptying, and the marks should get closer together. The hole size, the bottle's width and the room all change this, so the tuning step in e1 matters. In ch2, the sinking time of a plastic cup is the least sure part. It may need a hole near 2 millimetres and several tries. In a1, a neat tear gives a small difference between the two totals, so the step says to tear a wobbly edge and gives a backup. The sample numbers there and in the roots are examples, never results. The shadow clock (p1) needs a sunny sill and cannot be done on a cloudy week. The three bowls (a7) need cold water, which is easy in the fridge and harder in a hot monsoon week. Facts still to check against their sources: the coast figures of 7,516.6 and 11,098.8 kilometres and who published them; the Arthashastra passages (book 2, chapters 19 and 20); the Harappan weights, the brick proportions and the Lothal scale marks of about 1.7 millimetres; the metric law of 1956; the Jaipur sundial height and date; the caesium number; the 1889 cylinder, India's copy number 57 and the drift of about 50 millionths of a gram; the fingerprint comparison, which is a common claim and unverified; the Mars Climate Orbiter cost; the Gimli aeroplane; the 2020 body temperature study; the numbering of Kena Upanishad 1.6, which differs between editions; and the cost and lengths of the three videos once their ids are found. The sample readings in the maths problems are imagined, not measured. The three videos still need real ids. The sample numbers in the roots are examples, not results.

terms.meaning: To find out how much there is of something, as a number, by comparing it with a unit.
terms.example: You measure a table by laying your hand along it and counting how many hands fit.
terms.art: A child laying a hand span along a table edge and counting on her fingers.

terms.meaning: A fixed amount that we choose to compare other amounts with.
terms.example: One hand span is a unit. A table nine hand spans wide has been measured in that unit.
terms.art: A row of nine hand shapes along a table edge.

terms.meaning: A number together with its unit. The number alone says nothing.
terms.example: '5' means nothing. '5 centimetres' is the width of a matchbox.
terms.art: A card reading 5 with a question mark, then the same card reading 5 centimetres beside a matchbox.

terms.meaning: The distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger when your hand is spread wide.
terms.example: A child's hand span is shorter than a grown-up's, so the same table needs more of the child's spans.
terms.art: A spread hand drawn with a line from thumb tip to little-finger tip.

terms.meaning: A unit taken from part of the body, such as a finger width, a hand span, a forearm or a foot.
terms.example: A flower seller in Madurai measures jasmine strings by the length of her forearm.
terms.art: A seller holding a jasmine string along her forearm from elbow to fingertip.

terms.meaning: The part of the arm from the elbow to the wrist. As a unit, it is measured from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.
terms.example: In Tamil the forearm length is called a muzham, and some flower sellers still use it.
terms.art: An arm bent at the elbow with a line drawn from elbow to fingertip.

terms.meaning: A unit that many people agree to keep exactly the same, by copying it from one shared example.
terms.example: A metre is the same in Kochi and in Kolkata, so a tailor in one can sew for a customer in the other.
terms.art: Two shops in different cities holding identical metre sticks.

terms.meaning: An instrument that finds how heavy something is by setting it against known weights until the two sides match.
terms.example: Vegetables on one pan and metal weights on the other. When the beam is level, the two sides match.
terms.art: A two-pan balance with onions on one side, iron weights on the other and the beam level.

terms.meaning: A piece of metal made to a known mass, used on a balance. In daily talk, weight also means how heavy something is.
terms.example: A shopkeeper puts a one-kilogram weight on one pan and rice on the other.
terms.art: A small iron weight with a stamped seal on its base.

terms.meaning: A set of units built on the metre, the kilogram and the second. Bigger and smaller units are made by multiplying or dividing by ten.
terms.example: A doctor in Kochi and a doctor in Brazil both write a dose in milligrams and mean the same amount.
terms.art: A metre stick, a kilogram weight and a clock face side by side.

terms.meaning: The standard unit of length. It is about the distance from the floor to a door handle.
terms.example: A cricket pitch is a little over 20 metres long.
terms.art: A door with a metre stick laid from the floor to the handle.

terms.meaning: A short word put in front of a unit to make it bigger or smaller.
terms.example: Kilo in front of metre makes kilometre, which is 1,000 metres.
terms.art: The word kilometre split into kilo and metre with an arrow between them.

terms.meaning: A prefix that means one thousand.
terms.example: A kilogram is 1,000 grams, and a kilometre is 1,000 metres.
terms.art: A heap of 1,000 small dots next to the word kilo.

terms.meaning: A prefix that means one hundredth.
terms.example: There are 100 centimetres in one metre.
terms.art: A metre stick divided into 100 small marks.

terms.meaning: A prefix that means one thousandth.
terms.example: There are 1,000 millilitres in one litre, and 1,000 millimetres in one metre.
terms.art: A litre bottle beside a row of 1,000 tiny drops.

terms.meaning: How long something is from one end to the other.
terms.example: The length of a pencil is about 15 centimetres.
terms.art: A pencil beside a ruler with an arrow from end to end.

terms.meaning: A unit of length. One hundredth of a metre. A finger is about one centimetre wide.
terms.example: A matchbox is about 5 centimetres wide.
terms.art: A finger drawn beside a ruler's first centimetre.

terms.meaning: A unit of length. One thousandth of a metre. A fingernail is about one millimetre thick.
terms.example: The rain in India is reported in millimetres.
terms.art: A fingernail edge drawn beside the smallest marks of a ruler.

terms.meaning: A unit of length for journeys. One thousand metres.
terms.example: A road sign in India that says 'Madurai 40' means 40 kilometres.
terms.art: A roadside milestone with a town name and a number.

terms.meaning: A long, bendy strip with units marked along it. A tailor's soft tape goes round a body, and a steel tape rolls into a case.
terms.example: A tailor wraps a soft tape round a waist, which a stiff ruler cannot do.
terms.art: A tailor's soft tape curled round a rolled cloth.

terms.meaning: The amount of matter in something. Its standard unit is the kilogram.
terms.example: A one-litre bottle of water has a mass of about one kilogram.
terms.art: A bottle of water on a balance with a one-kilogram weight on the other pan.

terms.meaning: The standard unit of mass. One thousand grams.
terms.example: A packet of sugar in a shop is usually one kilogram.
terms.art: A packet of sugar next to a stamped one-kilogram weight.

terms.meaning: A unit of mass. One thousandth of a kilogram. A paper clip is about one gram.
terms.example: A letter at the post office is weighed in grams.
terms.art: A paper clip on one pan of a small balance.

terms.meaning: A unit of mass equal to 1,000 kilograms.
terms.example: A lorry is weighed in tonnes at a weighbridge.
terms.art: A lorry standing on a weighbridge with a number on a board.

terms.meaning: The amount of space something takes up.
terms.example: A tall thin tumbler and a short wide bowl can have the same volume.
terms.art: A tall tumbler and a wide bowl, both filled with the same amount of water.

terms.meaning: The usual unit of volume for liquids. It is the space inside a cube 10 centimetres along each edge.
terms.example: A bucket holds about 15 litres, and a packet of milk is often half a litre.
terms.art: A cube of 10 centimetres drawn beside a one-litre bottle.

terms.meaning: A unit of volume. One thousandth of a litre. A teaspoon holds about 5 millilitres.
terms.example: A cough syrup cap is marked at 5 and 10 millilitres.
terms.art: A small syrup cap with two lines marked on its side.

terms.meaning: A tall tube or jug with marks on the side, used to measure the volume of a liquid.
terms.example: A kitchen measuring jug works like a measuring cylinder.
terms.art: A clear tall jug with marks and water inside.

terms.meaning: What clocks measure. Nobody has a final account of what time is, only ways to count it.
terms.example: You measure how long an egg boils by counting minutes on a clock.
terms.art: A clock beside an egg in a pan.

terms.meaning: The standard unit of time. A slow clap takes about one second.
terms.example: Sixty seconds make one minute.
terms.art: A hand slowly clapping beside a second hand on a clock.

terms.meaning: Anything that repeats in a steady way and can be counted.
terms.example: A swinging pendulum, a dripping tap and the Sun's shadow can all be used as clocks.
terms.art: A swinging key on a thread, a dripping tap and a sundial shadow.

terms.meaning: A clock that uses water running out of a hole or into a bowl, so that the water's movement counts the time.
terms.example: In old India a copper bowl with a small hole floated in water and sank after one ghati.
terms.art: A floating bowl with a hole, half full of water, in a larger vessel.

terms.meaning: A clock that tells the time by the shadow of a pointer as the Sun moves across the sky.
terms.example: At the Jantar Mantar in Jaipur, built about 1730 CE, a sundial 27 metres tall can be read to about two seconds.
terms.art: A tall triangular sundial with a long shadow falling across a curved scale.

terms.meaning: A very exact clock that counts the waves given off by atoms.
terms.example: India's official time is kept by atomic clocks in New Delhi.
terms.art: A cabinet with a glowing tube and a display of numbers.

terms.meaning: How hot or cold something is, shown as a number on a thermometer.
terms.example: A hot summer afternoon in Nagpur can reach 45 degrees Celsius.
terms.art: A thermometer beside a cup of tea and a cup of cold water.

terms.meaning: The everyday unit of temperature. Water freezes at 0 and boils at 100 at sea level.
terms.example: A healthy body is about 37 degrees Celsius.
terms.art: A thermometer scale with marks at 0, 37 and 100.

terms.meaning: An instrument that measures temperature.
terms.example: A fever thermometer is put under the arm or in the mouth to read a child's temperature.
terms.art: A digital fever thermometer showing a number.

terms.meaning: Another scale of temperature. A healthy body is about 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit, which is about 37 degrees Celsius.
terms.example: Many fever thermometers in India show both scales.
terms.art: A fever thermometer with two scales side by side.

terms.meaning: A tool made to measure something, such as a ruler, a balance, a jug or a thermometer.
terms.example: A tailor's tape is an instrument for length.
terms.art: A ruler, a jug, a balance and a thermometer laid in a row.

terms.meaning: The smallest and largest amount an instrument can measure.
terms.example: A fever thermometer reads only from about 35 to 42 degrees Celsius.
terms.art: A thermometer scale with a bracket from 35 to 42.

terms.meaning: The smallest step marked on an instrument.
terms.example: A bathroom scale moves in steps of 100 grams, so it cannot show a 20-gram letter.
terms.art: A ruler with one tiny gap between two marks highlighted.

terms.meaning: The number you take from an instrument.
terms.example: You read 12.4 centimetres from a ruler when the pencil's tip is a little past the 12.4 mark.
terms.art: An eye looking straight at a ruler mark with an arrow to a written number.

terms.meaning: The mark where counting starts on an instrument. Check it before you measure.
terms.example: A kitchen scale must show 0 before you put anything on it.
terms.art: A kitchen scale with 0 on its screen and an empty pan.

terms.meaning: A careful guess at an amount, made by comparing it with something whose size you already know.
terms.example: A door is about 2 metres high, so a wall twice as tall is about 4 metres.
terms.art: A child holding up a thumb to judge the height of a door.

terms.meaning: The long, bendy line where the land meets the sea.
terms.example: India's coast runs round the south and both sides of the country.
terms.art: A map of an outline of land with a wavy coast.

terms.meaning: A careful measuring of land, using instruments, so that maps can be drawn.
terms.example: The Survey of India measures the country and makes its official maps.
terms.art: A surveyor beside a tripod instrument looking at a distant hill.

terms.meaning: A number that is found to be the same everywhere and at all times.
terms.example: Light in empty space always travels at 299,792 kilometres per second.
terms.art: A beam of light crossing a starry sky with a speed written beside it.

terms.meaning: How much is inside a packet, without the wrapping.
terms.example: A biscuit packet may show 60 g as its net quantity, however big the packet looks.
terms.art: A packet front with a corner circled that reads 60 g.

terms.meaning: Finding a size by measuring other things you can reach, such as angles and shadows, and then working it out.
terms.example: You can work out how tall a banyan stands from the length of a shadow on the ground, without climbing.
terms.art: A tree and a metre stick throwing shadows on the ground.

terms.meaning: How wide a corner is, or how far something has turned. A full circle is 360 degrees.
terms.example: The corner of a book is a right angle, which is 90 degrees.
terms.art: A book corner with a small square mark.

terms.meaning: The dark shape made when something blocks light.
terms.example: A stick standing in the sun makes a long shadow in the morning and a short one at noon.
terms.art: A stick on the ground with a shadow falling to the left.

terms.meaning: A number that physicists work out for a thing, which stays the same when things change and lets them predict what will happen. Science has no final account of what energy is.
terms.example: A cricket ball flying through the air has more energy than the same ball lying on the grass.
terms.art: A cricket ball in flight and the same ball resting on grass.

terms.meaning: The pull that draws things with mass towards each other. Einstein described it as the bending of space and time. Nobody yet has a theory that joins gravity with the physics of very small things.
terms.example: Gravity pulls a dropped ball down to the floor.
terms.art: A ball falling from a hand to the floor.

terms.meaning: The physics of the very small, such as atoms and the particles inside them, where things behave in ways that everyday life does not show.
terms.example: Quantum physics explains why a caesium atom gives off waves at one exact rate, which atomic clocks count.
terms.art: An atom drawn as a small cloud with waves leaving it.

experiments.title: The dripping bottle clock test: does a water clock keep steady time?
experiments.question: A bottle with a small hole near the bottom drips as the water runs out. Does the water level fall by the same amount in every 2 minutes?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the level fall by the same amount in each 2 minutes, or by different amounts? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The same bottle, the same hole, the same starting line and the same water are used from start to finish. Only the time changes. Every mark is made at a call from one phone stopwatch. If you have time, run the test a second time, because one run can be spoiled by a bump or a bubble. If you cannot, look for the same pattern in the first half and the second half of your one run.

materials.item: a clear plastic bottle of 1 litre with straight sides (a water or soft drink bottle), cap off
a sewing pin and a thin nail about 1 millimetre thick
a steel tumbler to stand the bottle on, upside down
a sink, a large tray or a basin to catch the water
a strip of paper about 3 centimetres wide and 20 centimetres long, and sticky tape
a 30 centimetre ruler and a pencil
a jug of water
a phone with a stopwatch
a folded towel and a cloth for spills

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the hole, with the bottle on a folded towel and the pin pushed away from their hands. Do the test over a sink or a tray, and wipe up spills at once so nobody slips. Use a plastic bottle, never glass. Pour the water on a plant afterwards.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Work out each fall by subtracting. Then write three sentences: what I thought would happen, what I saw, and why I think it happened. Last, write how many minutes one whole emptying took.
experiments.context: In this test you make a water clock from a bottle and find out whether it ticks evenly. The answer shows why old Indian water clocks were judged by one whole emptying and not by marks along the side.

setup.art: A grown-up pushing a sewing pin through the side of a plastic bottle, 2 centimetres above the bottom, with the bottle lying on a folded towel.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up makes one small hole in the side wall, 2 centimetres above the bottom.

setup.art: A bottle standing on an upside-down steel tumbler in a sink, with a paper strip taped up the side opposite the hole and a pencil line at 12 centimetres.
setup.caption: 2. Stand the bottle on the tumbler in a sink. Tape the strip on the side away from the hole, with its zero level with the hole.

setup.art: A thin jet of water leaving the hole and a phone stopwatch beside the bottle, with a finger ready over the hole.
setup.caption: 3. Fill to the 12 centimetre line. Lift your finger and start the stopwatch together.

setup.art: The paper strip taken off the bottle and laid flat with pencil marks closer and closer together towards the bottom.
setup.caption: 4. Mark the level on the strip at every call of 2 minutes. Lay the strip flat and look at the gaps.

flow.do: A grown-up lays the empty bottle on a folded towel. Find a spot on the straight side wall about 2 centimetres above where the bottom curves up. Push the sewing pin through the wall and twist it once, pushing away from your hands. Then stand the bottle on the upturned tumbler in the sink with the cap off. Tape the paper strip up the opposite side, with the bottom of the strip level with the hole. Draw a pencil line across the strip 12 centimetres above the hole.
