flow.say: A bottle with a hole is a clock if the water leaves at a steady pace. We will find out if it does. First, why do you think we put the strip on the side away from the hole?
flow.kid: A grown-up makes the hole with a pin. Stand the bottle in the sink. Tape a strip up the other side. Draw a line 12 centimetres above the hole.
flow.parent: Start with the sewing pin. A hole can be made wider but never smaller, so a small one is the safe start. The 12 centimetre line keeps the water level in the straight part of the bottle, below the sloping shoulder. The strip is on the far side so the water jet does not wet it.

flow.do: Tune the hole so that the bottle takes about 15 to 25 minutes to empty. Hold a finger over the hole and pour water to the 12 centimetre line. Start the stopwatch and lift your finger. After exactly 1 minute, mark the level on the strip and measure how far it fell. A fall of 1 to 1.5 centimetres in the first minute is right. If the fall is smaller, the hole is too small. A grown-up pushes the pin or the thin nail in again. The grown-up twists it once to widen the hole. Then you try again. If the fall is bigger, the hole is too big. Dry the bottle and press two layers of sticky tape over the hole. Then make a new hole with the pin about 3 centimetres to the side, and try again. Each try takes about 3 minutes, and most bottles need two or three.
flow.say: A clock that empties in 3 minutes is too quick for us to mark. One that takes an hour is too slow. We want the water to fall about a finger-width in the first minute. Is it falling too fast or too slowly?
flow.kid: Fill to the line and start the stopwatch. After 1 minute, measure the fall. Under 1 centimetre means widen the hole. Over 1.5 means tape it and make a new hole.
flow.parent: A fall of 1 to 1.5 centimetres in the first minute means one whole emptying takes roughly 16 to 24 minutes. That gives 8 to 12 marks. Water leaves a bottle faster when the water above the hole is deeper. So the first minute is the fastest, and the fall slows after that. Bottles differ in width and holes differ in size, which is why we tune instead of guessing.

check.q: The water fell 3 centimetres in the first minute. What should you do?
options: Cover the hole and make a smaller one
check.why: A fall of 3 centimetres a minute would empty 12 centimetres in about 8 minutes, which is too quick for marks every 2 minutes. A smaller hole slows the water. If you chose a wider hole, that would make the water run even faster.

flow.do: Refill the bottle to the 12 centimetre line while a finger covers the hole. Ask your child to say their guess and reason from the predict question. Write the guess down. Do not correct it.
flow.say: Will the water fall by the same amount in each 2 minutes? Say your guess and why you think so.
flow.kid: Say your guess and why you think so. Then wait for the stopwatch.
flow.parent: Children often say the water will fall by equal amounts, because a clock should tick evenly. That is a good guess. Write it down and let the bottle answer it.

flow.do: Lift your finger and start the stopwatch at the same moment. Each time the stopwatch shows 2, 4, 6 or 8 minutes, call 'mark'. Ask your child to draw a pencil line across the strip at the water level, and to write the minute next to the line. Carry on until the water stops falling, which happens when the level reaches the hole.
flow.say: When I call mark, draw a line where the top of the water is. Halfway through, tell me this. The water started 12 centimetres up. Half of that is 6 centimetres. Will the water be at 6 centimetres after half of the time? Say your guess.
flow.kid: Mark the water level every 2 minutes when your grown-up calls. Write the minute next to each line. Keep going until the water stops falling.

ask.q: At the halfway time of the whole run, is the water also half way down?
good: No. It has already fallen more than half.
It fell fast at the start, so the level is lower than the middle.

flow.parent: Marking is easier if one person watches the stopwatch and the other watches the water. If the water runs out in under 14 minutes or takes over 28, still finish the test and write the time. In your results, one whole emptying is the time from the first mark to the last. The level reaches 6 centimetres after only about 6 minutes of a 20-minute run.
flow.wait: Keep watching until the water stops falling

flow.do: Take the strip off and lay it flat. Measure from the zero line to each pencil line and write the levels in the table. Subtract to find each fall. Look at the falls from first to last. Then ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Last, write how many minutes one whole emptying took.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Measure each line from zero. Write the levels. Find each fall. Say what you thought, what you saw and why.

ask.q: Why did the falls get smaller?
good: Less water above the hole pushes less.
The water ran out slower as the bottle emptied.

ask.q: Could you use this bottle as a clock if you only ever used a whole emptying?
good: Yes, if it takes the same time on each try.
Each whole emptying could be one unit of time.

flow.parent: You should see the falls shrink: for example, about 2 centimetres between the first marks and well under 1 centimetre between the last. The exact numbers depend on your bottle. Water pushes out harder when more water sits above the hole, so the bottle runs fast when full and slowly when nearly empty. So it is an uneven clock, even though the water is running all the time. An old Indian water clock was not read by marks along the side. It was judged by one whole sinking of the bowl, which took the same time on each try. Your whole emptying time can be used the same way. What the test cannot tell us is whether the stopwatch is perfectly steady. We trust it because it agrees with other clocks, and those agree with the Sun and with atomic clocks. Ask your child how they could check a clock that they trust.
flow.think: If you filled the bottle only to half, would it take half as long to empty?

activities.title: The wiggly line test: does a smaller step give a longer edge?
activities.context: In this activity you measure the same torn paper edge with a big step and then a small step. You find out whether a wiggly edge has one length or many.

materials.item: an A4 sheet of paper to tear, and a second clean sheet
stiff card from a cereal box, for two strips
a ruler with millimetres and a pencil
scissors, used by a grown-up
about 60 centimetres of sewing thread

schedule.what: Tear and trace the edge, measure it with a 3 centimetre step, a 1 centimetre step and a thread, and compare.

activities.record: Write three lengths for your edge: with the 3 centimetre step, the 1 centimetre step and the thread. Under them, write the straight distance between the two ends. Then write one sentence on what happens as the step gets smaller.

setup.art: Two hands tearing a sheet of paper slowly down its length, with the torn edge zigzagging.
setup.caption: 1. Tear a sheet slowly in wobbly bites, so the edge zigzags.

setup.art: The torn piece lying on a clean sheet with a pencil tracing along its edge and a dot at each end of the pencil line.
setup.caption: 2. Trace the edge on a clean sheet. Make a dot at each end of the pencil line.

setup.art: A 3 centimetre card strip held with one end on a dot and the other end swung to touch the pencil line, with the next dot being made.
setup.caption: 3. Step along the line. Hold one end on the dot, swing the other end to the line, and make a new dot.

setup.art: A thread laid along the pencil line, then pulled straight beside a ruler.
setup.caption: 4. Lay a thread along the line, then pull it straight and measure it.

flow.do: Tear a sheet of A4 paper into two pieces, from the top edge to the bottom edge. Tear slowly, in bites about 1 centimetre long, and change direction a little with each bite, so that the torn edge zigzags. Lay the torn piece on the clean sheet. Run a pencil along the torn edge to trace it. Make a dot at each end of the pencil line.
flow.say: We are going to ask a plain question. How long is this edge? Before we measure, guess a number of centimetres.
flow.kid: Tear the paper slowly, in little wobbly bites. Trace the edge on the clean sheet. Put a dot at each end.
flow.parent: A neat, straight tear gives a small result, so tear deliberately wobbly. If your first edge looks nearly straight, tear another with bigger zigzags.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts two strips of card, one exactly 3 centimetres long and one exactly 1 centimetre long, each about 1 centimetre wide. Check each with the ruler.
flow.say: These strips will be our steps. One is long and one is short. Which do you think will give the longer answer?
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts two card strips, 3 centimetres and 1 centimetre. Guess which will give the longer answer.
flow.parent: Accurate strips matter more than neat ones. Measure the cut strip with the ruler and trim if needed.

flow.do: Start with the 3 centimetre strip. Put one end on the first dot. Swing the other end until it touches the pencil line, and make a dot there. Slide the strip so that its first end is on the new dot, and repeat. Count each step until you reach the far end of the line. Measure the small gap left at the end with the ruler. Work out the length: steps times 3, plus the gap. Do the same with the 1 centimetre strip.
flow.say: Count your steps out loud. The strip is always straight, so each step is exactly 3 centimetres in a straight line. Why might that skip some of the bends in the edge?
flow.kid: Step along the line with the 3 centimetre strip. Count the steps and measure the little gap at the end. Do it again with the 1 centimetre strip.
flow.parent: Expect the 1 centimetre steps to give a longer total than the 3 centimetre steps. For example, a child might get about 18 centimetres with 3 centimetre steps and about 24 with 1 centimetre steps. Your numbers will differ. If the two totals are within 2 centimetres, tear a more crumpled edge and try again, because the effect grows with the number of bends.

flow.do: Lay the thread along the pencil line, following every bend. Hold the thread at the far dot, pull it straight and measure it with the ruler. Then measure the straight distance between the two dots. Write all four lengths down in order of step size, from the biggest step to the smallest.
flow.say: You now have four answers for one edge. Which one is the real length? What do you notice as the steps get smaller?
flow.kid: Lay the thread along the line and measure it straight. Measure the straight distance between the dots too. Say what you notice as the steps get smaller.

ask.q: What happens to the length as the step gets smaller?
good: It gets longer.
A smaller step follows more bends.

ask.q: Which of your four answers is the real length of the edge?
good: Each is the length for that step size.
There is no single answer until we say how fine the measuring was.

flow.parent: The straight distance between the dots is the biggest possible step and gives the shortest answer. The thread follows the most bends and gives the longest. Each time the steps shrink, the total grows. The edge did not change. A real coast does the same, which is why India's coast has more than one length. What this test cannot tell us is whether the thread's answer is the true length. A thread also skips the tiny bends between the paper fibres. Ask your child what they would use to follow even smaller bends.

check.q: You make the step half as long. What do you expect the total to do?
check.why: A shorter step follows more of the bends, so the total grows. It grows by a small amount, not by double, because the long bends were already followed. If you chose the same, the edge would have to be smooth.

activities.title: Two hands, one table: why we need units that are the same for everyone
activities.context: In this activity a child and a grown-up measure one table with their own hands and then with a ruler. You find out why body units fail between people.

materials.item: a table, a desk or a floor mat about 1 metre wide
a ruler, a tailor's tape or a steel tape
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Measure one table with two people's hand spans, then with a tape, and compare.

activities.record: Write three lines: the table in the child's hand spans, the table in the grown-up's hand spans, and the table in centimetres. Then write one sentence on which of the three numbers two strangers could agree on.

setup.art: A child laying a spread hand again and again along a table edge, with a pencil dot at the end of each span.
setup.caption: 1. Measure the table's width in your own hand spans. Make a dot where each span ends.

setup.art: A grown-up doing the same on the same table, with a smaller number written beside the child's bigger one.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up measures the same table in their hand spans.

setup.art: A tape stretched across the table's width with the centimetre number read off.
setup.caption: 3. Measure the table with a tape and compare the three numbers.

flow.do: Ask your child to measure the width of the table with their hand span. Lay the spread hand flat with the thumb tip on the table's edge. Make a pencil dot at the little-finger tip. Move the thumb to that dot and repeat. Count the spans, and write the number. If a part of a span is left, say 'a bit more than'.
flow.say: Spread your hand wide and walk it across the table. Count how many spans. Write down the number.
flow.kid: Spread your hand wide. Step it across the table and count.
flow.parent: A table about 1 metre wide gives roughly 5 spans for a child and 4 for a grown-up. Whatever your numbers are, write them down exactly.

flow.do: Now measure the same table with your own hand span in the same way. Write your number next to your child's. Ask your child to say why the two numbers are different.
flow.say: Now I will measure the same table with my hand. Why do you think I get a different number from yours? Did the table change?
flow.kid: Watch a grown-up measure the same table. Why is their number different from yours?

ask.q: The table is the same. Why are the numbers different?
good: The hands are different sizes.
Each of us used a different unit.

flow.parent: The table did not change. Two different units gave two different numbers. If you have a forearm length to try, measure the table in forearms too, from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.

flow.do: Measure the table with a tape or a ruler and write its width in centimetres. Ask your child which of the three numbers two strangers could agree on, and why.
flow.say: Here are three numbers for one table. A shopkeeper in another city has never seen your hand. Which number could he understand?
flow.kid: Measure with the tape. Which number could a stranger understand?

ask.q: Which number could a stranger understand without ever meeting you?
good: The centimetres, because everyone has the same centimetre.
The tape number, because it is a shared unit.

flow.parent: Hand spans work well inside one family. They break down between people. That is why every trade needed a unit that was the same for all. If you have it, read the story 'How Big Is a Foot?' by Rolf Myller as a follow-up.
flow.think: Would a number in hand spans help if you were sewing a dress for someone far away?

activities.title: Guess first, then measure: how close can your guess get?
activities.context: In this activity you work out your own measuring anchors, guess the size of six things, and then check each guess with an instrument.

materials.item: a ruler or tape
a one-litre bottle of water
a tumbler and a measuring jug or a 5 millilitre spoon
a packet of rice, sugar or atta that shows its mass on the label
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Measure your anchors, guess six things, check them, and find which guesses came within a quarter.

activities.record: Make a table with four columns: the thing, my guess, the measured value and how far off I was. Circle every guess that came within a quarter of the true value.

setup.art: A child measuring her finger width, a door's height and a bottle with a ruler and tape.
setup.caption: 1. Find your anchors: your finger width, a door's height and a litre bottle's mass.

setup.art: A child holding a full water bottle in one hand and a bag of rice in the other and weighing each by feel.
setup.caption: 2. Guess each thing by comparing it with an anchor.

setup.art: A table with guess and measured columns and a tick beside the close guesses.
setup.caption: 3. Measure each thing and write how far off you were.

flow.do: Find your anchors. Measure the width of your finger with a ruler. Measure the height of a door with a tape, or know it is about 2 metres. Hold the full one-litre bottle of water so you know how 1 kilogram feels. Fill a teaspoon with water and remember that it holds about 5 millilitres.
flow.say: These are your anchors. A good guess starts by comparing a new thing with something whose size you already know. How wide is your finger?
flow.kid: Measure your finger. Hold the litre bottle. Remember a door is about 2 metres high and a teaspoon holds 5 millilitres.
flow.parent: Anchors are the sizes you carry with you. A finger is about 1 centimetre wide and a door is about 2 metres high. A full litre bottle is your kilogram. Do not tell your child the answers to the later guesses.

flow.do: Pick six things to guess. Use the width of a window, the length of the room and the height of a chair. Add the mass of the packet of rice, the volume of a tumbler of water and the volume of a cooking pot. Ask your child to guess each one, with its unit, and write the guess. Ask which anchor they used for each.
flow.say: Guess each one and tell me which anchor you used. A guess without a unit does not count.
flow.kid: Guess six things, with their units. Write each guess before you measure. Say which anchor you used.
flow.parent: Do not allow measuring until all six guesses are written. The unit is part of the guess. For the rice packet, hide the label until after the guess.

flow.do: Measure each thing. Use the ruler or tape for lengths, the label for the packet and the jug or spoon for the volumes. Write each measured value and work out how far off the guess was. A guess within a quarter of the true value, for example 75 to 125 when the true value is 100, is a good one.
flow.say: Now we measure. How far off was each guess? Which was closest, and which anchor did you use for it?
flow.kid: Measure each thing. Work out how far off you were. Circle the guesses within a quarter.

ask.q: Which of your six guesses was closest, and why?
good: The one near an anchor I knew well.
Comparing with a known size helped most.

flow.parent: Most children guess lengths well and volumes badly. That is useful to know. A tumbler usually holds 200 to 250 millilitres, which is 40 to 50 teaspoons.

flow.do: Look at the six rows. Ask your child whether a guess ever caught a mistake, such as reading a tape in the wrong unit. Ask which instrument they would pick to check a guess that is far off.
flow.say: If your guess is 2 metres and the tape says 20, what do you do?
flow.kid: Say what you would do if your guess and your tape were very different.
flow.parent: A guess works like a safety net. If it disagrees badly with the instrument, we check the unit, the zero and the reading before we trust either.
flow.think: Which of your guesses would you trust most if you could not measure it?

activities.title: Reading a ruler and a jug: the zero, your eye and the curved water
activities.context: In this activity you find three ways a reading can go wrong, with a ruler and a jug, and learn how to avoid each one.

materials.item: a ruler and a pencil
a clear plastic tumbler or a measuring jug
water

schedule.what: Measure from a non-zero mark, find how your eye changes a reading, and look at the curve of the water.

activities.record: Write what you found for each trap in one sentence: the zero, the angle of your eye and the curve of the water.

setup.art: A pencil lying beside a ruler with its end on the 1 centimetre mark and the other end read at 8.
setup.caption: 1. Start the pencil at the 1 centimetre mark. Read the other end and subtract.

setup.art: A child holding a pencil upright in front of a ruler and looking with one eye, then the other, with two dotted sight lines.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the pencil upright in front of the ruler. Look with one eye, then the other.

setup.art: A clear tumbler of water seen from the side with the water edge curving up the glass and an eye level with the flat middle.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the water's surface from the side at eye level.

flow.do: Look at your ruler. Find the zero mark and see if it is at the very end or a little way in. Lay a pencil along the ruler with its end on the 1 centimetre mark, not the zero. Read where the other end reaches. Subtract 1 to find the pencil's length. Then slide the pencil back so its end sits on the zero mark and read again. Compare the two lengths.
flow.say: A measurement starts counting from a mark. Where does your ruler start counting? What happens if you start the pencil somewhere else?
flow.kid: Put the pencil's end on the 1 centimetre mark. Read the other end. Take away 1. Then put the end on zero and read again.
flow.parent: Both ways give the same length when you subtract the starting mark. This is the habit of starting at zero or, when you cannot, writing down where you started. If your ruler's zero is a little in from the end, point that out now. Aligning the ruler's end instead of the zero mark gives a reading too small by that gap.

flow.do: Hold a pencil upright about 10 centimetres in front of the ruler, with the ruler lying flat on the table. Close one eye and note which mark the pencil seems to touch. Open that eye and close the other. Note the mark again. Then look straight down from above and say which mark the pencil really touches.
flow.say: Which mark does the pencil sit against when you look with your left eye? And with your right? Why would two people reading the same ruler give two numbers?
flow.kid: Hold the pencil in front of the ruler. Look with one eye, then the other. The pencil seems to jump along the ruler.

ask.q: Why does the pencil seem to jump?
good: Each eye looks from a different place.
We see the pencil against a different part of the ruler.

flow.parent: The pencil seems to jump a few centimetres, because your two eyes are about 6 centimetres apart. Reading a ruler or a jug from one side makes the mark seem to shift. The fix is to bring your eye level with the mark and look straight on.

flow.do: Pour water into the tumbler to about halfway. Put it on a level table. Bend down so your eye is level with the water's surface. Look at how the water meets the glass. Then read the jug's mark at the flat middle of the surface. Try reading from above and from below, and write each reading.
flow.say: Look at where the water touches the glass. What shape does it make? Which part of the water do you read?
flow.kid: Bend down until your eye is level with the water. Look at the water's edge. Read the flat middle.
flow.parent: Water climbs the glass slightly at the edge, so the surface is a shallow curve. Read the flat bottom of the curve. Reading from above or below can shift a reading by 10 or 20 millilitres in a small jug.
flow.think: Why might two people get different readings from the same jug?

activities.title: Too thin, too lumpy: one sheet of paper and a stone
activities.context: In this activity you find the thickness of one sheet of paper and the volume of a stone. A ruler or a jug cannot measure either of them directly.

materials.item: a book with at least 100 leaves, such as a thick notebook or a paperback
a ruler with millimetres
a stone or a steel nut or a marble that sinks, about the size of an egg or smaller
a tall straight clear tumbler and a pen
a 5 millilitre spoon or a medicine cap
thread to lower the stone

schedule.what: Measure a stack of paper and divide, then measure a stone by the rise of water.

activities.record: Write the thickness of the pages, the number of leaves and the thickness of one leaf. Then write how many spoons of water the stone made the level rise by, and the stone's volume.

setup.art: A ruler pressed against the side of a stack of pages and a finger pointing at the thickness reading.
setup.caption: 1. Measure the thickness of the page block, not the cover. Count the leaves.

setup.art: A tumbler of water with a pen line at the water level and a stone hanging on a thread above it.
setup.caption: 2. Mark the water level. Lower the stone in on a thread.

setup.art: The stone taken out and a spoon pouring water until the level reaches the second pen line.
setup.caption: 3. Mark the new level. Take the stone out and add spoons of water up to the new line.

flow.do: Open the book and find the page numbers. A leaf is one sheet with a page on each side, so the number of leaves is half the number of pages. Press the page block flat and measure its thickness in millimetres, without the covers. Divide the thickness by the number of leaves. Write the thickness of one leaf.
flow.say: A ruler cannot measure one sheet of paper. It is too thin. But it can measure a hundred of them together. How might that help?
flow.kid: Count the leaves. Measure the stack. Divide the thickness by the number of leaves.
flow.parent: For 200 pages and a block 20 millimetres thick, one leaf is 0.1 millimetre. Your book will differ. Measure the pages pressed flat, as the glue edge may be thicker.

flow.do: Pour water into the tumbler until it is about 5 centimetres deep. Mark the level on the outside with a pen. Tie the thread to the stone and lower it into the water. Mark the new level. Take the stone out. Add spoons of water, counting each, until the water reaches the second mark. Multiply the spoons by 5 to find the stone's volume in millilitres.
flow.say: The stone has no neat edges, so a ruler is no use. Where does the water go when the stone goes in? How can we measure that?
flow.kid: Mark the water, then lower the stone and mark again. Take the stone out. Add spoons of water up to the new mark, and count the spoons.
flow.parent: The water rises by exactly the stone's volume, because the stone pushes water aside to make room. If the stone makes the level rise by less than 5 millimetres, use a bigger stone or a narrower tumbler. A level teaspoon holds about 5 millilitres. If the stone floats, press it under with the thread.
flow.think: What would happen to the water level if the stone were twice as big?

activities.title: Packet detective: how much is really inside, and what does it cost for each 100 grams?
activities.context: In this activity you read the net quantity on kitchen packets and find which packet gives the most for your money.

materials.item: three food packets from the kitchen, such as biscuits, atta, tea or milk, with a price and a net quantity on each
a strip of tablets from a medicine box, if you have one
paper, a pencil and a phone calculator

schedule.what: Read the net quantity and price on three packets, and work out the price for each 100 grams or millilitres.

activities.record: Make a table with the packet, its net quantity, its price and the price for each 100 grams or millilitres. Circle the cheapest for its size.

setup.art: Three food packets on a table with a finger pointing to the small print that says net quantity.
setup.caption: 1. Find the net quantity and the price on each packet.

setup.art: A phone calculator dividing a price by a mass and a table with a result column.
setup.caption: 2. Work out the price for each 100 grams or millilitres.

setup.art: Three packets lined up from biggest to smallest and then from most to least inside.
setup.caption: 3. Line the packets up by how big they look, and by how much is inside.

flow.do: Find the words 'net quantity' or 'net weight' on each packet. Write the amount and the unit: grams, kilograms, millilitres or litres. Write the price too. If you have a medicine strip, find the milligrams printed on it.
flow.say: Every packet must say how much is inside, without the wrapping. Find it and say the unit.
flow.kid: Find the net quantity on each packet. Write the number with its unit. Write the price.
flow.parent: The net quantity is in the small print, often at the bottom or near the price. The law in India requires it. If a packet gives mass in kilograms, change to grams by multiplying by 1,000.

flow.do: For each packet, divide the price by the net quantity in grams. Then multiply the result by one hundred. That gives the price for each 100 grams. Use a phone calculator if needed, and write the result in the table.
flow.say: Which packet looks the cheapest? Now check. How much would 100 grams of each cost?
flow.kid: Divide the price by the net quantity. Multiply the result by one hundred. Write the price for 100 grams.

ask.q: Which packet gives the most for each rupee?
good: The one with the lowest price for each 100 grams.
We have to divide, because the packets are different sizes.

flow.parent: For example, a 60 gram packet that costs 10 rupees costs about 16.7 rupees for each 100 grams. A 250 gram packet that costs 45 rupees costs 18 rupees. The bigger packet is not always the better price.

flow.do: Line the packets up from biggest looking to smallest looking. Then line them up from most inside to least inside. Compare the two lines.
flow.say: Does the biggest packet always hold the most? Why might a packet look big and hold little?
flow.kid: Line up the packets by size. Then line up by how much is inside. Are the lines the same?
flow.parent: Air, a tray and a wrapper all take up space in a packet. The net quantity is the number to trust, not the size of the packet.
flow.think: Why is it better to look at the net quantity than at the size of the packet?

activities.title: Three bowls of water: why hands are poor thermometers
activities.context: In this activity you put one hand in cold water and one in warm water. Then you put both in the same middle bowl, and see why we use a thermometer.

materials.item: three steel bowls or large steel tumblers
cold water from the fridge or with ice, room-temperature tap water and comfortably warm water
a thermometer, if you have one
a towel

activities.safety: The warm water must be only as warm as a child's bath. A grown-up tests it with an elbow or a thermometer and never uses hot water from a kettle straight from the boil.

schedule.what: Fill three bowls, put each hand in a different bowl, then both hands in the middle bowl, and say what you feel.

activities.record: Write what the left hand felt and what the right hand felt in the middle bowl. Write what a thermometer says, if you have one.

setup.art: Three bowls in a row labelled cold, middle and warm with a hand over each.
setup.caption: 1. Fill three bowls: cold, middle and comfortably warm.

setup.art: A child with her left hand in the cold bowl and her right hand in the warm bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Keep the left hand in the cold bowl and the right hand in the warm bowl for one minute.

setup.art: Both hands in the middle bowl with a puzzled face and two thought bubbles saying warm and cool.
setup.caption: 3. Put both hands in the middle bowl and notice what each hand feels.

flow.do: A grown-up fills three bowls. Fill one with cold water from the fridge or with a few ice cubes, one with ordinary tap water and one with comfortably warm water. Test the warm bowl with your elbow to check it is not hot.
flow.say: Three bowls, three temperatures. Before we try, what will the middle bowl feel like to each hand?
flow.kid: A grown-up fills three bowls: cold, middle and warm. Guess what the middle bowl will feel like.
flow.parent: Use cold tap water if there is no fridge water, and let it run for a minute. The warm bowl should feel pleasantly warm, never hot. Do not let a child pour hot water.

flow.do: Put your left hand in the cold bowl and your right hand in the warm bowl. Keep them there for one minute. Then take both hands out and put both into the middle bowl at once.
flow.say: One minute in cold on the left and warm on the right. Now both hands go into the middle bowl. What does each hand tell you?
flow.kid: Left hand in the cold bowl, right hand in the warm bowl, for one minute. Then both hands into the middle bowl.

ask.q: The middle bowl is one temperature. What does each hand say, and what does that show?
good: The left hand says warm and the right hand says cool.
Our skin tells us how the water compares with our hand, not the temperature.

flow.parent: The left hand, used to the cold, feels the middle bowl as warm. The right hand, used to the warm, feels it as cool. The water is the same. Skin senses change, not a fixed number.

flow.do: If you have a thermometer, put it in the middle bowl and read it. Tell your child that this one number is the same for everybody. Ask what the numbers are for if we can already feel hot and cold.
flow.say: The thermometer says one number. Why would we want a number, when we can feel the water?
flow.kid: Read the thermometer in the middle bowl. Say why a number helps.
flow.parent: For many centuries hot and cold were only feelings. It took people about two hundred years to make a thermometer that everyone agreed on. A number lets two people in two places agree. If you have no thermometer, skip the reading and discuss the question.
flow.think: What else do we feel that is hard to turn into a number?

activities.title: Is your pulse a steady clock?
activities.context: In this activity you count your pulse while sitting and after star jumps, and find out whether the heart can be used as a clock.

materials.item: a phone with a timer
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Find the pulse, count it for 30 seconds sitting, then again after 20 star jumps, and compare.

activities.record: Write the beats for 30 seconds sitting, then double them for one minute. Do the same after star jumps. Write which was faster.

setup.art: A child with two fingers on her wrist and a phone timer on the table.
setup.caption: 1. Find your pulse with two fingers on your wrist or neck.

setup.art: A child counting beats while a phone shows 30 seconds.
setup.caption: 2. Count the beats for 30 seconds while sitting quietly.

setup.art: A child doing star jumps and then sitting with fingers on her wrist again.
setup.caption: 3. Do 20 star jumps and count again.

flow.do: Sit quietly. Put two fingers, not the thumb, on the inside of the other wrist below the thumb, or on the side of the neck. Press gently until you feel a regular tap. That is your pulse.
flow.say: Your heart pumps blood each time it beats, and you can feel each beat in your wrist. Can you find it?
flow.kid: Sit still. Put two fingers on your wrist or neck. Find the tap.
flow.parent: If it is hard to find, try the neck, beside the windpipe. Use fingers and not the thumb, because the thumb has its own pulse.

flow.do: Set a timer for 30 seconds. Count the beats while sitting quietly. Write the count and double it for beats in a minute.
flow.say: Count each tap. When the timer rings, stop. How many beats in 30 seconds? How many in a minute?
flow.kid: Count beats for 30 seconds. Double the number for a whole minute.
flow.parent: A sitting child usually has about 70 to 110 beats in a minute. A different number is fine. A child may lose count. Count together and compare.

flow.do: Do 20 star jumps. Sit down and count the beats for 30 seconds again. Write the count and double it. Compare the two results.
flow.say: Is your pulse the same after jumping? Could you use it as a clock to time an egg?
flow.kid: Do 20 star jumps. Sit and count for 30 seconds again. Which was faster?

ask.q: Could you use your pulse as a clock? Why or why not?
good: It speeds up and slows down, so it is not steady.
A clock must tick the same way each time.

flow.parent: The pulse is a rough clock. It is useful, but it speeds up after exercise or excitement. A clock needs to repeat in a steady way. This is why a better clock was always searched for.
flow.think: What would you need to make a pulse into a trustworthy clock?

projects.title: A shadow clock on a sunny sill: does the shadow come back to the same marks?
projects.context: In this project you make a shadow clock from a pencil and a card. You mark where the shadow tip falls each hour, and check on later days whether the marks still work.

materials.item: a sheet of card about the size of a notebook page
a pencil and a ball of plasticine or clay to hold it upright
paper tape or sticky tape
a window sill, balcony or terrace that gets sun for most of the day
a phone to check the time

projects.safety: Look at the shadow and never at the Sun. Keep children away from the edge of a balcony or terrace.

schedule.what: Set up the card in the morning and mark the shadow's tip every hour through the day.
At the same hours, check whether the shadow tip falls on the same marks.
Label the marks as a scale and compare with the phone's time.

projects.record: Draw a table with the hour and the mark number. On day 2 add whether the shadow tip fell on, near or far from each mark. On day 3 write which marks agreed most.

setup.art: A card on a sunny sill with a pencil standing in a ball of plasticine and the card's outline traced in pencil on the sill.
setup.caption: 1. Tape the card on a sunny sill. Stand the pencil upright in plasticine.

setup.art: The same card with a small dot marking the tip of the shadow and a written hour beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Every hour, mark the tip of the pencil's shadow and write the hour.

setup.art: A row of dots on the card forming a curve with hour labels.
setup.caption: 3. The dots make a curve. Next day, check whether the shadow lands on the same dots.

flow.do: In the morning, put the card on the sunniest part of the sill. Trace its outline on the sill with a pencil so it can go back to the same place. Tape the card down. Press a ball of plasticine on the card and stand the pencil upright in it. Check that the pencil is straight up and does not wobble.
flow.say: A pencil in the Sun makes a shadow. As the Sun moves across the sky, the shadow moves. We will mark its tip each hour and see if it works like a clock.
flow.kid: Tape the card to a sunny sill. Stand a pencil upright in plasticine. Do not move the card again.
flow.parent: Choose a sill that is in the Sun at least from 9 in the morning to 3 in the afternoon. The card and pencil must not be moved all day. If the pencil leans, the marks will be wrong.

flow.do: At each full hour from 9 in the morning to 3 in the afternoon, make a small dot at the tip of the pencil's shadow. Write the time beside the dot. If a cloud hides the Sun, mark when it comes out and write the real time.
flow.say: Where is the tip of the shadow now? Mark it and write the time. Is the shadow longer or shorter than the last time?
flow.kid: Every hour, put a dot at the tip of the shadow. Write the time beside it.
flow.parent: Each mark takes about 2 minutes. Use a phone alarm so you do not forget. The shadow is longest in the morning and evening and shortest around noon, when the Sun is highest.
flow.wait: Come back each hour through the day

flow.do: On the second morning, check that the card and pencil are still on the traced outline. At each of the same hours, look at where the shadow tip falls. Say whether it lands on the mark for that hour, near it or far from it.
flow.say: The Sun went round the sky yesterday and again today. Does the shadow land on the same marks at the same hours?
flow.kid: Check the shadow tip at the same hours as yesterday. Does it land on the marks?
flow.parent: The shadow should fall within a few millimetres of the marks, as the Sun's path changes very slowly from day to day. On cloudy days, wait for the next sunny one. If marks seem off by more than a centimetre, the card may have moved.
flow.wait: Come back on the next day at the same hours

flow.do: Draw a line through the dots to join them. Write the hours along it so it is a scale. Compare the shadow's time with the phone's time at three hours on day 3. Say how close the shadow clock was.
flow.say: Your shadow clock has a scale now. How close was it to the phone? Who made the first clocks like this?
flow.kid: Join the dots and write the hours. Check three times against the phone. How close was your clock?

ask.q: What makes a shadow clock work as a clock?
good: The Sun moves in a steady way across the sky.
It repeats each day, so the marks can be counted.

flow.parent: This is how sundials work. The great sundial at the Jantar Mantar in Jaipur, built about 1730 CE, uses the same idea at a size of 27 metres. A sundial reads solar time, which can differ from the clock by several minutes through the year.
flow.think: What would a shadow clock do on a cloudy day, and what could you use at night?

challenges.title: A home-made balance that can tell a 5 gram difference
challenges.context: This is a design problem. You build a balance from things at home and use water as your known weights to find the mass of an object.
challenges.problem: Build a balance that can weigh a small thing, such as a tomato or a mango, to the nearest 10 grams, using only things from home. A millilitre of water has a mass of about one gram, so water can serve as your known weights. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: Use only things you can find at home. A kitchen scale may be used only to check your result at the end.
The empty balance must hang level before you weigh anything.
Use water, measured with a spoon or syrup cap, as your known weights.
Weigh the same object twice and see if the answers agree.
materials: a clothes hanger, or a 30 centimetre ruler and thread
two small paper cups or plastic cups
a 5 millilitre spoon or a syrup cap with marks
water and a tomato or a mango

setup.art: A clothes hanger hanging from a door handle with a paper cup tied to each end by thread.
setup.caption: 1. Hang a clothes hanger with a cup on each end.

setup.art: A hand adding a little tape to one cup until the hanger sits level.
setup.caption: 2. Add small bits of tape until the empty balance sits level.

setup.art: A tomato in one cup and a spoon adding water to the other cup.
setup.caption: 3. Put the tomato in one cup. Add spoons of water to the other until the balance is level.

flow.do: Hang the hanger from a door handle or a hook. Tie a cup to each end with thread, at the same distance from the middle. Check that the hanger hangs level. If one side drops, add small pieces of tape to the lighter side until it sits level.
flow.say: A balance can only tell you that two sides match. First make the empty balance match. What do you do if one side drops?
flow.kid: Hang the hanger. Tie a cup on each end. Add bits of tape to the light side until it hangs level.

ask.q: Why must the balance be level before you weigh anything?
good: Otherwise one side starts out heavier.
We need both sides to match when empty.

flow.parent: If the cups hang at different distances from the middle, the balance is unfair. Measure each thread's place from the centre with a ruler.

flow.do: Put the tomato in one cup. Use the 5 millilitre spoon to add water to the other cup, one spoon at a time, until the hanger sits level again. Count the spoons. Multiply by 5. That is the tomato's mass in grams, because a millilitre of water has a mass of about one gram.
flow.say: Pour water spoon by spoon until the two sides match. How many spoons? How many grams is that?
flow.kid: Put the tomato on one side. Add spoons of water on the other side until the hanger is level. Count the spoons and multiply by 5.
flow.parent: A medium tomato weighs about 80 to 120 grams, so you will pour about 16 to 24 spoons. If the hanger bends and the beam wobbles, steady it with a finger. A syrup cap that holds 10 millilitres makes it faster.

flow.do: Weigh the same tomato again from scratch. Compare the two answers. If you have a kitchen scale, check your answer against it. Write the difference.
flow.say: Did the two weighings agree? How big is the difference? What would you change to make it smaller?
flow.kid: Weigh the tomato again. Do the answers agree? Check with a kitchen scale if you have one.
flow.parent: Answers within 10 or 20 grams are a good result. A bigger gap means the cups were uneven or the hanger was not level. Check the level first.

flow.do: Try one change to make the balance better, such as longer threads, a lighter hanger or smaller water spoons. Weigh the tomato again. Say whether the answers got closer together.
flow.say: What is one thing that would make your balance tell smaller differences?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Weigh again. Did the answers get closer?
flow.parent: A smaller spoon, a lighter beam and a smoother pivot all help. Change only one thing at a time, so you know what made the difference.
flow.think: Could your balance ever be exactly right? What would be left over?

general: An equal-arm balance from a hanger or a ruler, with water as the known mass. Check that it is level when empty, then match.
Use a smaller spoon, so that the water you add is in smaller steps and the match is closer.
Check your answer against a shopkeeper's scale or a kitchen scale.
creative: A rubber-band scale. Hang a cup from a rubber band, add 20 millilitres of water at a time and mark how far the band stretches. Then use your marks to read any object's mass.

A floating-cup scale. Float a plastic cup in a bucket, add 50 millilitres of water at a time, and mark how low the cup sinks each time. Then put your object in the cup and read its mass off the marks.
A seesaw with unequal arms. A long arm with a small amount of water balances a heavy thing on a short arm. Work out the ratio of the arms to find the mass.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own balance or scale in a way not listed here. How small a difference in mass can it show? What limits it, and how could you test that?

challenges.title: A sinking-bowl clock like the old Indian ghati bowl
challenges.context: This is a design problem. You make a floating cup with a small hole that sinks after a set time, like the copper bowl that old Indian timekeepers used.
challenges.problem: Make a clock from a plastic cup with a pinhole, floating on water in a bucket, that sinks in about 5 minutes. Three runs should agree within 30 seconds. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: Use a plastic cup, never glass or a steel katori, so a grown-up can safely make the hole.
Float the cup upright each time, and let it fill by the hole alone.
Time at least three runs, and write each one.
Compare your cup with a phone stopwatch, which is the clock you trust.
materials: a small plastic cup that holds 150 to 250 millilitres, such as a curd cup
a bucket or large steel vessel at least 15 centimetres deep, filled with water
a sewing pin and a thin nail
sticky tape, a pencil and paper

setup.art: A grown-up pushing a nail through the middle of the bottom of a plastic cup.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up makes a small hole in the middle of the cup's bottom.

setup.art: An empty plastic cup floating upright in a bucket of water.
setup.caption: 2. Float the cup upright in the bucket.

setup.art: A cup half sunk in a bucket with water coming in through its bottom hole and a phone stopwatch beside the bucket.
setup.caption: 3. Start the stopwatch and watch the cup fill and sink.

flow.do: A grown-up makes one hole in the middle of the bottom of the cup with the sewing pin, pushing away from the hands. Float the cup upright in the bucket and see that it floats on a level keel. If it tips, press a small ball of plasticine in the bottom of the cup to steady it.
flow.say: Long ago, an Indian timekeeper floated a copper bowl with a small hole in a vessel of water. The bowl filled slowly and sank after exactly one ghati, which is 24 minutes. We will make a smaller one. Why does the cup need a hole?
flow.kid: A grown-up makes one hole in the cup's bottom. Float the cup upright in the bucket.
flow.parent: Make the first hole with the sewing pin. A hole can be widened and never made smaller. A cup that tips can fill from the top instead of the hole, so keep it upright.

flow.do: Float the cup. Start the stopwatch as soon as it floats upright. Watch the cup fill through the hole. Stop the stopwatch when the rim goes under the surface. Write the time. Empty the cup and try again twice more, writing each time.
flow.say: How long did the cup take to sink? Was the second run the same as the first?
flow.kid: Float the cup. Start the stopwatch. Stop when the cup sinks. Do it three times.
flow.parent: Expect a long first time if the hole is small, such as 10 to 30 minutes. Do not wait more than 10 minutes. Go straight to the tuning step if the cup has not sunk by then. A run in which the cup tips over should be thrown away and done again.

flow.do: Tune the cup. If it takes more than 6 minutes, or does not sink in 10, a grown-up twists the thin nail in the hole once to widen it. If it takes under 4 minutes, a grown-up covers the hole with two layers of sticky tape on the outside. Then the grown-up makes a new hole with the pin about 2 centimetres away. Run again after each change.
flow.say: Too slow means the hole is too small. Too fast means it is too big. What will you change?
flow.kid: Too slow: ask a grown-up to widen the hole. Too fast: ask a grown-up to tape it and make a smaller hole.
flow.parent: Aim for between 4 and 6 minutes. A thin nail makes a hole of about 1 millimetre. A wider hole may be needed for a 5-minute cup, so expect two or three tries.

flow.do: Do three timed runs with the tuned cup. Write each time. Work out the gap between the longest and the shortest. Say whether the cup is steady within 30 seconds.
flow.say: Are your three runs close together? What would you change to make a better clock?
flow.kid: Time three runs. Work out the gap between the longest and the shortest.
flow.parent: The old bowls were judged by whether they sank in the same time on every run, not by being exactly 24 minutes. A clock is good when it is steady and then checked against a better one.
flow.think: If your three times were 4.9, 5.1 and 5.0 minutes, would you trust the cup? What else would you check?

general: Tune the hole size by widening or taping and re-piercing until the sink time is about 5 minutes.
Keep the cup upright with a ball of plasticine inside the bottom, so that it fills only through the hole.
Run three times and use the middle value.
creative: Use a steel katori and have a grown-up drill a hole, as the old timekeepers did, and compare with the plastic cup.
Make the same clock with two different holes, and mark on a chart which one makes a 5-minute clock and which makes a 10-minute one.
Fill a second cup with water to its brim, float it and time how long it takes to fill the remaining space. Use this to make an hour clock from many bowls.
challenges.your_turn: Make a clock of your own design that takes about 10 minutes, using anything at home. How will you check that it keeps the same time on each run?
challenges.safety: A grown-up makes the holes, with the cup on a folded towel and the pin pushed away from their hands. Use a plastic cup, never glass. Empty the bucket on a plant afterwards.

games.title: Closer Than You: an estimating game for two or more
games.context: In this card game every player guesses the size of something, with its unit. Then the card is turned over to show the real size. The closest guess scores the most points.

setup.art: A table with 24 cut-out estimate cards in a pile, face down, and a pencil and paper for each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 24 cards and shuffle them. Put them face down in a pile.

setup.art: Two players each writing a guess on their own piece of paper with a hand covering it.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over the top card. Each player writes a guess with its unit, keeping it covered.

setup.art: A card turned over to show the true size and a score sheet with points written in.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over to show the real size. Score each guess.

items.f: How long is the long side of an A4 sheet of paper?
items.b: 29.7 centimetres, almost 30. A school ruler is 30 centimetres long, so the sheet is about one ruler.

items.f: How wide is the short side of an A4 sheet of paper?
items.b: 21 centimetres. It is about two-thirds of a school ruler.

items.f: How high is an ordinary door?
items.b: About 2 metres. Your own height is a useful anchor: most doors are a little over a grown-up.

items.f: How long is a cricket pitch?
items.b: 20.12 metres. That is 22 yards, or about 20 long strides.

items.f: How far is Chennai from New Delhi by rail?
items.b: About 2,180 kilometres. A fast train takes more than a day to cover it.

items.f: What is the mass of one litre of water?
items.b: 1 kilogram. This is why a full one-litre bottle is a good anchor for a kilogram.

items.f: What is the mass of the gas in a full household cooking cylinder?
items.b: 14.2 kilograms. It is the gas only, without the steel.

items.f: How much does a teaspoon hold?
items.b: About 5 millilitres. A tumbler holds about 40 to 50 teaspoons.

items.f: How much is in a small packet of milk?
items.b: 500 millilitres, which is half a litre.

items.f: How much does a household bucket hold?
items.b: About 15 litres, or 15 full one-litre bottles.

items.f: How many seconds are in one hour?
items.b: 3,600. There are 60 seconds in a minute and 60 minutes in an hour, and 60 times 60 is 3,600.

items.f: How many minutes were in one ghati?
items.b: 24 minutes. Sixty ghatis made a day and a night.

items.f: At what temperature does water boil at sea level?
items.b: 100 degrees Celsius. This is one of the two fixed marks of the Celsius scale.

items.f: What is a healthy body temperature?
items.b: About 37 degrees Celsius, which is 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit.

items.f: What is the mass of a newborn baby?
items.b: About 3 kilograms, as heavy as three litres of water.

items.f: How thick is a fingernail?
items.b: About 1 millimetre.

items.f: What is the mass of a paper clip?
items.b: About 1 gram. A thousand clips make about 1 kilogram.

items.f: How high is Mount Everest?
items.b: 8,848.86 metres, which is nearly 9 kilometres.

items.f: How far is it round the Earth?
items.b: About 40,000 kilometres, which is what Eratosthenes worked out about 240 BCE from a shadow.

items.f: How tall is the great sundial at the Jantar Mantar in Jaipur?
items.b: 27 metres, about the height of a nine-storey building.

items.f: How many beats does a sitting child's heart make in a minute?
items.b: About 70 to 110. It is faster after running.

items.f: How many kilograms are in one tonne?
items.b: 1,000. A lorry is weighed in tonnes.

items.f: How many millimetres are in one metre?
items.b: 1,000. Milli means one thousandth.

items.f: What is the mass of one tola of gold?
items.b: About 11.7 grams. A tola is an old Indian unit that jewellers still sometimes use.

printables.title: Score sheet, to copy by hand: ten rows for the ten cards, with columns for each player's guess, how far off, and points
items: Card 1. Guess, how far off, points.
Card 2. Guess, how far off, points.
Card 3. Guess, how far off, points.
Card 4. Guess, how far off, points.
Card 5. Guess, how far off, points.
Card 6. Guess, how far off, points.
Card 7. Guess, how far off, points.
Card 8. Guess, how far off, points.
Card 9. Guess, how far off, points.
Card 10. Guess, how far off, points.

rules: Shuffle the 24 cards and put them face down. Each game uses 10 cards.
Turn over the top card so that everyone sees the question but not the answer on the back.
Each player writes a guess with its unit on their own paper, and says out loud which anchor they used. A guess with the wrong unit scores 0, and a guess with no unit scores 0.
When all guesses are written, show them together. Then turn the card over to read the true size.
Work out how far off each guess was, as a part of the true size. Within one tenth scores 3 points. Within a quarter scores 2 points. Within a half scores 1 point. More than that scores 0.
The closest guess on the card also earns 1 extra point. If two guesses are equally close, both get it.
Play 10 cards. The player with the most points wins. If two players tie, play one more card.
If you play alone, play 10 cards and try to beat your own score next time.
If a guess and the true size differ a lot, say how you would check which is right with an instrument.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards from the printed sheet. Shuffle them and put them face down. Take a sheet of paper and a pencil for each player.
flow.say: We guess the size of ordinary things, with their units. The closest guess earns the most points. Why do you think the unit is part of the guess?
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Put them face down. Each player takes paper and a pencil.
flow.parent: Cutting is for the grown-up if the child is under 8. Keep the cards in an envelope after the game.

flow.do: Play one practice card together. Turn over the top card. Each player writes a guess with its unit. Show your guesses. Read the answer and score as in the rules.
flow.say: Say your guess with its unit. Which anchor did you use? Then we will see how close you got.
flow.kid: Practise with one card. Write a guess and its unit. See how close you are.
flow.parent: Practise scoring once, because the fractions are the hardest part. Within one tenth means for example 90 to 110 when the true size is 100.

flow.do: Play 10 cards. Each player guesses with a unit, shows the guess, and then the card is turned. Work out the points for each player after each card and write them on the score sheet.
flow.say: What is your guess? Which anchor did you use? Is it close?
flow.kid: Guess each card with its unit. Score the points.

ask.q: When a guess was far off, which anchor did you use?
good: An anchor that did not fit the thing.
I did not have an anchor for that size.

flow.parent: Let children argue for their guess. Two different anchors can both be defensible, such as a hand for a table or a door for a wall. The point is to say why.

flow.do: Add up the points. Talk about which card was the hardest, and which anchor helped most.
flow.say: Which size was hardest to guess, and why? Which anchor was the best?
flow.kid: Add up the points. Say which card was the hardest.
flow.parent: Very big sizes, such as the Earth, are hard to guess. A good habit is to say the unit first and then think about what size of number fits it.
flow.think: Which size would you like to be able to guess well, and how could you practise?

items.p: A recipe says 'add 2 of salt'. What is missing?
items.why: A number alone does not say how much. Two teaspoons and two kilograms are very different. If you chose another option, ask 'two what?' every time you see a number.

items.p: 1 kilometre is ____ metres.
items.why: Kilo means one thousand, so 1 kilometre is 1,000 metres.

items.p: A pencil is 15 centimetres long. In millimetres that is ____.
items.why: There are 10 millimetres in each centimetre, so 15 × 10 = 150.

items.p: Match each of these to the thing it measures best.
items.why: Each of these measures one kind of quantity: length, mass, volume, time or temperature.

items.p: Sort each one by what is being measured.
items.why: Length is how long, mass is how much matter, and volume is how much space.

items.p: Two people measure the same table in hand spans. They must get the same number.
items.why: False. Hands differ in size, so the numbers differ. The table did not change, but the unit did.

items.p: Which instrument suits measuring round a pot?
items.why: A soft tape bends round a curve, and a stiff ruler cannot. A scale measures mass, not length.

items.p: A bathroom scale that moves in steps of 100 grams can weigh a letter of 20 grams.
items.why: False. The scale's smallest step is bigger than the letter, so it would show 0 or one step. A kitchen scale with 1 gram steps can do it.

items.p: Put these in order from smallest to largest.
items.why: A millimetre is a thousandth of a metre, a centimetre a hundredth, and a kilometre is a thousand metres.

items.p: Give three times in your day when a guess is not good enough. Say what could go wrong with a guess.
items.a: A good answer names three real moments, such as medicine for a baby, buying rice or catching a train. It says what a guess could cost: harm, money or time.
items.why: People measure when two people must agree or a mistake is costly.

items.p: Draw a measuring jug being read. Show where your eye is and which part of the water you read.
items.a: A jug with marks, an eye drawn level with the water, and an arrow pointing to the flat middle of the surface.
items.why: An eye level with the mark and the flat part of the water gives a true reading.

items.p: A bag holds 2.5 kilograms of rice. How many grams is that?
items.why: Each kilogram is 1,000 grams, and 2.5 × 1,000 = 2,500.

items.p: You guess a door is 2 metres high. The tape reads 20. What now?
opts: Believe the tape. Doors are 20 metres.
Check the unit and the reading. The guess warns of a mistake.
items.why: A sensible guess catches errors. The tape may be in decimetres, or read from the wrong mark. Trusting the tape without checking would have made a silly answer.

items.p: Two ways to sell cloth.

views.who: A weaver who sells by the forearm (an imagined view)
views.says: My forearm needs no tool. I can measure anywhere, and it suits my customers.

views.who: A cloth inspector who uses a metre (an imagined view)
views.says: A metre is the same for everyone. Strangers can trust it, and a buyer can check it.

items.ask: Which would you use for a sale between two strangers? Which for a sale inside one family?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says the forearm suits people who know each other and a shared metre suits strangers, because it gives the same number to everyone.
items.why: Both are real ways of measuring. The trade-off is convenience against agreement.

items.p: Why do traders prefer a unit that is the same for everyone?
opts: Strangers get the same number for the same cloth
items.why: A shared unit lets two people agree on an amount without arguing. Being easy to carry or cheap are not the reason a standard unit exists.

items.p: A tablet holds 250 milligrams of medicine. In grams that is ____.
items.why: Milli means a thousandth, so 250 milligrams is 250 ÷ 1,000 = 0.25 grams.

items.p: Two readings of one jug are 240 and 260 millilitres. What is the likeliest cause?
opts: One reader looked from above and one from below
items.why: The angle of the eye shifts where a mark seems to be. Bring your eye level with the water. A jug does not change size between readings.

items.p: A stack of 100 sheets is 10 millimetres thick. One sheet is ____ millimetres.
items.why: 10 ÷ 100 = 0.1. A ruler cannot read one sheet, but it can read a hundred.

items.p: A fever thermometer that reads 35 to 42 degrees can measure boiling water.
items.why: False. Boiling water is 100 degrees, far beyond its range. Choose an instrument whose range covers your thing.

items.p: Match each instrument to the job it suits best.
items.why: The job decides the instrument: its range and its smallest division must suit the thing.

items.p: You must weigh 30 grams of spice. Which scale is best?
items.why: A kitchen scale moves in steps of about 1 gram. A bathroom scale's steps of 100 grams are bigger than the spice.

items.p: Put these in order from the finest smallest step to the coarsest.
a: a jeweller's balance that reads 0.001 gram
a kitchen scale with 1 gram steps
a bathroom scale with 100 gram steps
items.why: The smaller the step, the finer the instrument. A weighbridge is made for lorries, not letters.

items.p: A friend says a measurement is exact if the instrument is good. Do you agree? Use one example.
items.a: A good answer says no: every instrument has a smallest division, so a reading can only be as fine as that step. For example, a ruler in millimetres cannot tell 12.34 centimetres from 12.36.
items.why: Every measurement has a limit set by the instrument's smallest step and by the person reading it.

items.p: Draw a thermometer scale from 30 to 42 degrees with a mark every degree. Show where 37 is.
items.a: A line with 13 marks labelled 30 to 42, and a clear arrow or dot at 37.
items.why: A scale needs a start, a range and equal steps, and a fever thermometer covers only what a body needs.

items.p: Should the whole world use only metric units?

views.who: A scientist at a national measuring laboratory (an imagined view)
views.says: One system prevents costly mistakes and lets everyone share results.

views.who: A carpenter who works in inches (an imagined view)
views.says: Inches halve and quarter easily, and my craft grew up with them. Why should I change a method that works?

items.ask: Which view would you give most weight in a laboratory? Which in a carpenter's workshop?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer notes that both agree science needs one system, and they disagree about daily life, where old units carry the knowledge of a craft.
items.why: This is a real disagreement about what is gained and lost when old units are given up.

items.p: Why does a smaller step give a longer coast?
opts: It follows more of the bends
items.why: A long step jumps over bays and creeks. A short step goes into more of them, so the total grows. The coast itself does not change.

items.p: The edge of a steel plate gets much longer when you measure it with a finer ruler.
items.why: False. A smooth edge has hardly any bends to skip, so a finer step changes the answer very little. The puzzle belongs to jagged things.

items.p: How many metres are in 2,180 kilometres?
items.why: Each kilometre is 1,000 metres, and 2,180 × 1,000 = 2,180,000.

items.p: A spacecraft was lost in 1999 when numbers were read in the wrong unit. What would have helped?
opts: Writing the unit with every number and checking it
items.why: The numbers were right and the units were missing. A measurement is a number and a unit together.

items.p: A school gives one mark for a whole term of learning. Name two things the mark shows and two it leaves out.
items.a: A good answer names things the mark shows, such as spelling or sums. It also names things the mark leaves out, such as curiosity, kindness, effort or how well a child can explain.
items.why: A number is useful and incomplete. What it leaves out is part of what we know.

items.p: A baby is 3.2 kilograms. In grams that is ____.
Sort each by what a finer measuring step does to its length.
items: the edge of a steel plate
the edge of a banyan leaf
items.why: Smooth edges have few bends, so a finer step finds few new ones. Jagged things have bends at every size.

items.p: A tape shows whole centimetres. Readings of 82, 83 and 82 are averaged to 82.3. What is wrong?
opts: The tape cannot show tenths, so 82.3 claims too much
items.why: An average can have more digits than the tape, but it cannot honestly claim more precision than the tape's step. It is better to say about 82 centimetres.

items.p: A kitchen scale shows 5 grams with nothing on it. You add rice and it shows 255. How much rice?
items.why: The scale started at 5 and not at 0. Subtract the starting value: 255 − 5 = 250. Choosing 255 ignores the zero error.

items.p: A balance tells you a thing's mass without any known masses to compare.
items.why: False. A balance only says that two sides match. The known masses on the other side give the answer.

items.p: Two of the world's best clocks disagree by a tiny amount. Describe two ways people could decide what to do.
items.a: A good answer might say: compare both with a third clock, or compare many clocks and take an average, or agree which one to call correct. The key idea is that without a better clock, people must agree.
items.why: A clock is checked by comparing it with other clocks, so trust is built by agreement.

items.p: Why does a shop weight get checked against an inspector's weight?
opts: It is only for the law
It ties every kilogram of rice to the same shared kilogram
items.why: A chain of checks leads from the shop up to a national laboratory, so a kilogram means the same in every shop. It is more than a rule. It is how strangers trust each other.

items.p: Is knowledge poor if it cannot be measured?

views.who: Lord Kelvin, in a lecture of 1883
views.says: If you can put what you speak of into numbers, you truly know it. If you cannot, your knowledge is thin.

views.who: A field naturalist who watches animals for years (an imagined view)
views.says: I learnt what these animals are like by patient watching, before any numbers. Numbers can give false confidence.

items.ask: Which view fits how you know when a friend is sad? Which fits how you know how tall the friend is?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says both help, in different ways: numbers suit things that can be compared by an instrument, and careful watching suits things that cannot.
items.why: Scientists still disagree about how far measuring reaches. Neither view is marked right.

items.p: Put these in order from the shortest time to the longest.
items.why: A ghati is 24 minutes, which is more than a second and less than an hour.

items.p: A car wheel is 2 metres round. It turns 750 times. How many kilometres has the car gone?
items.why: 750 turns × 2 metres = 1,500 metres, which is 1.5 kilometres.

items.p: Why do doctors ask for children's doses in millilitres only?
opts: Spoons differ in size, so one number gives different doses
items.why: A kitchen spoon can hold much more or much less than another. A marked cap or syringe is the same for everyone.

items.p: A torn edge gave longer totals with smaller steps. What would 1 millimetre steps give? Why can it not grow for ever?
items.a: A good answer predicts a longer total, because the step follows more bends. It also says the growth must stop at some size, such as when the step is smaller than the paper's fibres.
items.why: Real edges are not infinitely jagged, so the growth slows. How fast, and where, depends on the thing.

items.p: Draw a wiggly coast and show how a long step and a short step give different totals.
items.a: A wavy line with a few long straight steps across it, and many short steps following the bends. The short steps add up to more.
items.why: A long straight step jumps over bays. A short step follows the bends, so the total is longer.

items.p: When you put your hand in warm water and then lukewarm water, your skin always gives you the true temperature.
items.why: False. Skin senses change. Lukewarm water feels cool after warm water and warm after cold. A thermometer gives the same number to everyone.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Foot, hand span, forearm, metre.
items.a: The metre. The other three are body units that differ from person to person. The metre is the same for everyone.
items.why: A standard unit is copied from one shared example. A body unit goes with the body.

items.p: A cold thermometer is put into a small cup of warm water. What may happen to the water?
opts: It cools a little, so measuring changed it
items.why: The thermometer takes a little warmth from the water. For small amounts, measuring changes the thing measured a little.

items.p: A 400 gram packet costs 60 rupees and a 1 kilogram packet costs 140. Which is cheaper for each 100 grams?
items.why: 60 ÷ 4 = 15 rupees for each 100 grams, and 140 ÷ 10 = 14. The bigger packet is cheaper here. Comparing the totals alone would not show this.

items.p: Sort each by whether it has a standard unit and instrument.
items: the heat of a cup of tea
items.why: Length, temperature and time have units and instruments. For beauty, kindness and pain, scientists still argue about whether any unit could be agreed.

quiz.p: Which job needs a measurement rather than a guess?
opts: Choosing a seat on a bus
quiz.why: Too much medicine can harm a baby, and two people must agree on the dose. A puddle or a seat is safe to guess.

quiz.p: A road sign says 'Madurai 40'. Why might a visitor from abroad be puzzled?
opts: The sign needs a longer name
They may expect miles, not kilometres
quiz.why: A number needs its unit. Locals know the unit, and a visitor from a country that uses miles may not.

quiz.p: What do you do when you measure a table?
opts: Guess, then check with a friend
Choose a unit, then count how many fit
Find the real width hiding in the table
quiz.why: A measurement is a unit and a count. There is no hidden 'real width' without a unit to compare with.

quiz.p: Which is true about the prefix milli?
quiz.why: Milli means a thousandth, so it takes 1,000 of them to make the whole. A hundred is the prefix centi.

quiz.p: A one-litre bottle of water has a mass of about 1 kilogram. What is the mass of 500 millilitres?
quiz.why: 500 millilitres is half a litre, so its mass is half a kilogram, which is 500 grams.

quiz.p: A thermometer is marked from 35 to 42 degrees. Which job does it suit?
quiz.why: A body is between about 35 and 42 degrees, which is the instrument's range. Boiling water and a freezer are far outside it.

quiz.p: A ruler's zero mark is 3 millimetres in from its end. A pencil starts at the ruler's end and reaches 14.0 centimetres. How long is it?
quiz.why: The pencil starts 3 millimetres before the zero mark, so it is 14.0 plus 0.3, which is 14.3 centimetres. Reading from the end hides the gap.

quiz.p: A torn edge is stepped with 3 centimetres and then with 1 centimetre. What happens to the total?
opts: It stays the same, as the edge did not change
It gets longer, as the small step follows more bends
It gets shorter, as small steps are more exact
quiz.why: A smaller step follows more of the bends, so the total grows. The edge did not change, but the way of measuring did.

quiz.p: Which is true of every measurement?
opts: It is exact if the tool is good
It is always the same for everyone
It cannot see finer than the instrument's smallest step
quiz.why: Every instrument has a smallest step, and no reading can be finer than that. A good tool makes the step small but not zero.

opts: A guess catches a mistake such as a wrong unit
A guess gives the exact answer
quiz.why: If the guess and the tape disagree a lot, you check the unit, the zero and the reading. A guess is a safety net.

quiz.p: Using a teaspoon holds 5 millilitres, what is a tumbler of water likely to hold?
quiz.why: A tumbler holds about 40 to 50 teaspoons, which is 200 to 250 millilitres. 25 millilitres is only five teaspoons.

quiz.p: Which of these can a thermometer not tell you?
opts: How hot a cup of tea is
The temperature of a child's forehead
How uncomfortable the heat feels to someone
quiz.why: A thermometer gives a number for temperature. It cannot tell how that heat feels to a person, which has no unit.

quiz.p: Someone says that old definitions of the kilogram, such as a metal cylinder, were fine for ever. What is a good reply?
opts: An object can change or be lost, so a constant of nature is steadier
quiz.why: A cylinder can lose atoms, be scratched or be lost. A constant of nature is the same everywhere, so any laboratory can make the unit again.

quiz.p: Which is a fair thing to say about a school mark?
opts: It shows everything a child has learnt
It is a number that leaves out much of what was learnt
It is false because numbers are false
quiz.why: A mark is useful, but it turns a whole term into one number. What it leaves out is part of what we know.

maths.problem: A paperback's pages are 2.4 centimetres thick and have 120 leaves. Find the thickness of one leaf in millimetres. A ruler reading can be wrong by up to 0.5 millimetre. How big is that error for one leaf measured alone, and for one leaf found from the stack?
maths.answer: 0.2 millimetre for one leaf. An error of 0.5 millimetre on one leaf is bigger than the leaf. From the stack it spreads over 120 leaves, which is about 0.004 millimetre.
maths.explain: 2.4 cm = 24 mm, and 24 ÷ 120 = 0.2 mm. Measured alone, a 0.5 mm error is more than twice the 0.2 mm leaf. In the stack, 0.5 ÷ 120 ≈ 0.004 mm.
maths.context: This problem uses a stack of pages to find a thickness that a ruler cannot read on one sheet.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a big measurement by a count shrinks the reading error by the same count, which is why stacks and averages are used for tiny things.

maths.problem: Imagine a bottle clock with the water level at 12.0, 9.7, 7.7, 5.9 and 4.3 centimetres at 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 minutes. Find the fall in each 2 minutes. What pattern do you see, and what would the falls be for an even clock?
maths.answer: 2.3, 2.0, 1.8 and 1.6 centimetres. The falls shrink each time. An even clock would fall by the same amount each time, for example 1.2 centimetres if it emptied 12 centimetres in 20 minutes.
maths.explain: 12.0 − 9.7 = 2.3, 9.7 − 7.7 = 2.0, 7.7 − 5.9 = 1.8 and 5.9 − 4.3 = 1.6. Each fall is a little smaller than the one before. An even clock covering 12 cm in 20 minutes would fall 12 ÷ 10 = 1.2 cm every 2 minutes.
maths.context: This problem uses imagined readings from a bottle clock to test whether it ticks evenly.
maths.why_maths: An even clock has equal changes in equal times. Subtracting each reading from the one before is how the unevenness shows.

maths.problem: A packet of 60 grams of biscuits costs 10 rupees. Another packet of 250 grams costs 45 rupees. Find the price for each 100 grams of each. Which is cheaper for its size?
maths.answer: About 16.7 rupees for each 100 grams for the small packet, and 18 for the big one. The small packet is cheaper for its size.
maths.explain: 10 ÷ 60 × 100 ≈ 16.7 rupees. 45 ÷ 250 × 100 = 18 rupees. The two packets have different sizes, so compare a price for the same amount.
maths.context: This problem compares two packets by finding the price for the same amount of each.
maths.why_maths: Equal amounts are the only fair basis for comparing prices. Dividing finds a price for one common amount.

maths.problem: Two towns are about 800 kilometres apart. The Sun's rays reach the ground at angles that differ by 7.2 degrees between them. A full circle is 360 degrees. Work out the distance round the Earth. What would it be if the angle were 7.5 degrees?
maths.answer: About 40,000 kilometres. With 7.5 degrees it would be about 38,400 kilometres.
maths.explain: 360 ÷ 7.2 = 50, so 800 km is one fiftieth of the way round, and 800 × 50 = 40,000 km. With 7.5 degrees, 360 ÷ 7.5 = 48, and 800 × 48 = 38,400 km.
maths.context: This problem follows the idea of Eratosthenes, who found the size of the Earth from an angle and a distance, using round numbers.
maths.why_maths: A part of a circle is the same fraction of the circle's distance as of its angle. This ratio lets us find a size nobody can stretch a tape across.

maths.problem: Imagine a coast measured with steps of 100 kilometres takes 30 steps, and with steps of 10 kilometres it takes 420 steps. Find the two lengths. How many times more steps? How many times longer is the coast?
maths.answer: 3,000 kilometres and 4,200 kilometres. There are 14 times more steps. The coast is 1.4 times longer.
maths.context: This problem uses imagined step counts to show how a coast's length grows as the step shrinks.
maths.why_maths: A step ten times smaller makes the length grow but not ten times. Comparing the two ratios shows the pattern of a jagged edge.
