spotted.text: At a tailor's shop, watch the tailor measure. Notice that she uses a soft tape, writes the numbers in a book, and often measures a second time before cutting.

spotted.text: Beside a road, look at a milestone or a sign with a town and a number. Notice that it says kilometres, and that the number goes down as you get closer.

spotted.text: Look at the clock in your home and at the clock on your phone. Notice that they may differ by a minute. Ask how each was set, and what they were checked against.

spotted.text: Look at two rulers or tapes. Notice where each one starts, and whether the zero is at the very end or a little way in.
spotted.art: The ends of two rulers lying side by side, with different zero positions.

applications: Cooking in many South Indian homes follows ratios in one cup. Idli batter is often made with about two or three tumblers of rice for one of urad dal. The size of the tumbler does not matter, because the same unit is used for both.

Medicine for children is measured in millilitres with the marked cap or a syringe. A kitchen spoon can hold twice as much as another, so doctors ask for the cap. Check the cap's lines before you give any dose.

At a petrol pump the display must show zero before the petrol starts, and the pump's meter is checked by the Legal Metrology department. This is the same habit as checking the zero of a ruler or a scale.

The India Meteorological Department reports rain in millimetres. One millimetre of rain means a litre of water on each square metre of flat ground. A straight-sided jar left outside can show the depth.
A plot of land may be advertised in cents, gunthas or bighas. Ask the seller to write the area in square metres too, so that two plots can be compared in one measure.

Surveyors measure what they cannot reach by angles and distances. The maps of the Survey of India, from roads to mountain heights, rest on many measured angles and on a base line measured with great care.
ask_kids: What is the longest thing you measured today, and what unit did you use? Why not a different one?
If you measured your height in hand spans, would your answer be the same as your friend's? What would you do about it?
Which of the things you do each day could you not do properly without a measurement?
Is there something in your day that no instrument could measure? How do you know it is there?
Which clocks do you trust, and what do you trust them against?
If a visitor from another world had a different unit for length, what could the two of you still agree on?

warmup.q: What are the two parts of a measurement?
How many metres are in a kilometre?
What does the prefix milli mean?
What is the standard unit of mass?
What is the standard unit of time?
Why check the zero of an instrument before you measure?
warmup.a: If it does not start at zero, every reading is wrong by the same amount.

warmup.q: Why is a smaller step better for measuring a jagged edge?
warmup.a: It follows more of the bends. But the total grows and does not settle.

warmup.q: Why do we use a stack of sheets to find the thickness of one sheet?
warmup.a: A ruler cannot read one sheet, so we measure many and divide.

quiz: A measurement needs both a number and a unit.
Five alone says nothing. Five centimetres is the width of a matchbox.
Two people measuring one table with their own hand spans must get the same number.
Hands differ, so the numbers differ. The table has not changed.
A kilogram is a thousand grams.
Kilo means one thousand.
A smaller measuring step gives a longer answer for a wiggly edge.
A small step follows more bends.
Hands are good thermometers.
Skin senses change, so one bowl can feel warm to one hand and cool to the other.
The metre was first defined from the size of the Earth.
In the 1790s it was one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator.
A bathroom scale can weigh a letter of 20 grams.
Its smallest step is far bigger than the letter.
A measuring jug should be read from above.
Read it with your eye level with the water, at the flat middle of the surface.
The kilogram is now defined from a constant of nature.
Since 2019 it has been tied to the Planck constant.
An estimate is only useful if it is exact.
A guess catches big mistakes and helps you choose an instrument.
odd: The first three are body units that differ from person to person. The metre is shared.
A second measures time. The others measure mass, length and volume.
A ruler, a soft tape and a steel tape all measure length. A jug measures volume.
The first three are jagged at every size. A steel plate edge is smooth.
A sundial, a water clock and a pulse all repeat and can be counted as clocks. A ruler measures length.
